maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
speechtext: I am desired by prominent gentlemen in Nova Scotia who are interested in the question of daylight saving to ask the right hon. the Prime Minister whether the Government have considered the passing of any legislation in regard to this matter. It is pointed out that Great Britain, Denmark, and Sweden have passed such legislation. As the right hon. gentleman is probably aware, in the city of Halifax and some other municipalities in Nova Scotia this has been put into effect.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
speechtext: Very few representations have come to the Government on this subject, and we have not yet considered it very fully. It seems that the local authorities, in most of the provinces at least, have the power to deal with it themselves, and if that be the case it may be that the matter had better be left to public opinion in the various localities.

maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
speechtext: The difficulty suggested by those interested in the project is in regard to the official closing of public institutions under the control of the Dominion Government, more particularly in connection with railways, which would not be under the control of the local authorities. It therefore might require Dominion legislation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DAYLIGHT SAVING.
speechtext:
I am not at all
sure that legislation will be necessary, because it may be possible for the departments of the Government, if it is thought desirable, to have regard to the local determination of the matter. However, I shall give my hon. friend's suggestion the best consideration I can between now and the next session.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF PAPER EXPORTS.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF PAPER EXPORTS.
speechtext: Is the rumour prevailing in Montreal this morning to the effect that the Government intends to pass an Order in Council to prohibit the exportation of paper and pulp to the United States true? I am told that a deputation met the Government yesterday or this morning.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROHIBITION OF PAPER EXPORTS.
speechtext: It has not been considered, so far as I am aware.

maintopic: THE DAVIDSON COMMISSION.
THE DAVIDSON COMMISSION.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: THE DAVIDSON COMMISSION.
speechtext: In the absence of my right hon. friend yesterday, I inquired if it was the intention to give the Opposition the privilege of counsel before the Davidson Commission on the charges brought the other day by the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie).

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE DAVIDSON COMMISSION.
speechtext:
I think it was announced by the Minister of Justice and also 'by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that if the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria, or my right hon. friend, should desire to be represented by counsel before the Davidson Commission, we would not only suggest, but recommend to Sir Charles Davidson that such counsel be allowed to appear. The position up to the present has been that Mr. John Thompson, K.C., was selected by Sir Charles Davidson to represent the people of Canada before that commission. So far as I am aware, he has discharged his duties with great ability, thoroughness, and impartiality. It may further be observed that he has done so without any remuneration whatever except an ordinary allowance for travelling expenses when he has been absent from the city of Ottawa. He has regarded hie work as a patriotic duty. I am informed that Mr. Thompson, in view of the criticism that has been passed upon him in this House, does not feel it coneis-

tent with his self respect that he should continue to discharge those duties. It may therefore be necessary for the Government to take some action towards appointing counsel to take his place. So far as counsel to represent the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria is. concerned, as I have already said, we shall not only suggest but recommend to Sir Charles Davidson that counsel be allowed to appear.
Sir WILFRID T,MIRIER: On the same terms as Mr. Johnston?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE DAVIDSON COMMISSION.
speechtext: As far as remuneration is concerned? We shall not make any undertaking with regard to that at the present time. I think it should be left for future consideration as was the case in connection with the Tarte-Langevin charges. There was no undertaking in advance, on the part of the Government at that time. The hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria undertook at once, in the same motion, to censure the Government and to demand an inquiry. He is at liberty to appear before the commission by his counsel and to proceed as he deems fit. The other question which my right hon. friend raised will be considered afterwards. Possibly some gentleman will be found on the other side who will undertake the duty upon the same terms as those upon which Mr. John Thompson undertook it.

maintopic: EXTENSION OF TERM OF PARLIAMENT

speechtext: The Orders of the day:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: EXTENSION OF TERM OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
My right hon. friend made inquiry yesterday during my absence about the joint resolution passed by this House and by the Senate in regard to the extension of Parliament. I have no further information than that which I gave some time ago. The joint resolution of the House and of the Senate went forward from the office of His Royal Highness the Governor General in the ordinary way, very shortly after it was passed. As soon as the revised Hansard was- available, containing the debates in both the House of Commons and in the Senate, I despatched them in a letter to Sir George Perley, stating to him that they contained the grounds upon which this House and the Senate had thought it desirable to pass the resolution, and directing him to place that information at the disposal of the Colonial Secretary.
Sir WILFRID LAUR1ER:	Has there
been any further communication?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: EXTENSION OF TERM OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I have had no further communication except an acknowledgement from Sir George Perley of my letter, and a statement that the information so afforded would be communicated to the Colonial 'Secretary. If desired, I shall send a cablegram inquiring as to the present position of the matter.

maintopic: EXTENSION OF TERM OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Certainly I
think that should be done. We want to know where we are with regard to this matter.	,

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.

speechtext: On the motion of Hon. J. D. REID (Acting Minister of Railways and Canals), the House went into committee on Bill No. 101, to authorize the acquisition of lines of railway between the city of Quebec and Naim Falls and between Lyster and St. Jean des Chaillons; Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
In accordance with the
arrangement that was made last night, I wish to discuss briefly a matter which is really more connected with the Customs Department than with the Department of Railways.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The arrangement was that
as soon .as we got through this Bill the other Estimates would come on, and then we could take up the other matter which has been mentioned.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: That was not the arrangement, as I understood it. The minister asked if I was ready to go on, and I said I would leave it altogether to the minister whether I would go on last night or this afternoon. It will not take very long to discuss this matter, and I have been waiting now for about two months to do so.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I wanted to proceed with this Bill last evening and I said that we would get through with the Bill last night and take up the Estimates to-day, and on the Estimates of any department we could take up this matter relating to the Customs Department I never had in mind that we would bring up on a Bill of this kind any matter connected with the Estimates; and I say now that as soon as this Bill is passed we can take up the matter on one of the items in the Estimates still remaining.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
This Bill may never
pass. I do not want the item that I wish to discuss to depend on the passing of this Bill. I have been waiting here, attending closely to the sessions of the House in order to bring the matter up when my hon. friend had his Customs Estimates under consideration; but, unfortunately, although I have been away only two days during this session, I was not here when that item was passed. I have been present here day after day for the last month or so waiting for this item to come up, and I would like it to be taken up now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I hope my hon. friend will see the impossibility of discussing Estimates on a Bill of this kind. Even if this Bill did not pass, the Estimates must pass, and there are some items remaining upon which my hon. friend will be at full liberty to discuss the subject which he has in mind.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
With Tegard to this Bill, I would hope that the Minister of Railways has considered favourably the suggestion that the judge of the Exchequer Court should allow only the actual, reasonable and necessary cost of the railway, less the cost of putting in order the road which has been in a large measure destroyed toy nonusage, which cost the engineer estimates at about $350,000, and also less the Dominion subsidies. I think that if the roads are to be taken over, that would be a fair basis on which the judge of the Exchequer Court could determine the amount to be allowed. I stated yesterday the reasons why I thought that the same action should be taken as is taken under the Act of 1915; but, if some basis of value is to be laid down for the guidance of the judge of the Exchequer Court which is to a large extent to tie his hands, I think he should be limited in the way I have suggested.
This is especially desirable by reason of what appears in the correspondence which has been brought down toy the Acting Minister of Railways this morning. That correspondence discloses a somewhat unusual condition of affairs, in that we have here an offer made by the Quebec Light, Heat and Power Company to give a clear title to the railway, free of all liens or liabilities whatsoever, for the sum of $2,500,000. That is dated 20th October, 1915. There is another offer from the same company to sell the Quebec and Saguenay railway in its present condition for the sum of $3,473,000 free of all encumbrances, and to sell the road upon

the south side known as the Lotbiniere and Megantic railway, free of all liabilities of every kind, for the sum of $330,000. The total of these three amounts upon which the companies offered to give a clear title would be in the vicinity of a million dollars less than what the acting minister proposes.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Well, $622,000 less; that is a very large sum. I observe, too, in the correspondence that there is a letter dated 2nd May from the President of the road, in which he says that some mistake toad 'been made. It seems extraordinary that, when the companies were making a formal offer to the Government for the sale of the road, they should have asked some $620,000 less than they subsequently discovered they ought to 'have asked for these roads. I think my hon. friend the Minister of Railways will agree that that very circumstance requires some careful consideration, particularly when it is proposed to tie the hands of the Judge of the Exchequer Court and to lay down for him a basis upon which the amount shall be assessed. My hon. friend the Solicitor General pointed out reasons why the Judge of the Exchequer Court should not be required simply to fix the value of the railway, and indicated the difficulties which would confront the judge if he were to determine the amount upon a basis like that. It would be difficult, toe pointed out, to determine what the actual value of-the road was. Therefore the minister proposes that it should be upon the basis of cost. If it is to be upon the basis of cost, and the Judge of the Exchequer Court should be so limited, it seems to me that it ought to be upon the basis of actual, reasonable, and necessary cost, because in that way he would toe able to fix approximately the value, whereas, if he is to be guided by the actual cost of the road, one can very readily see that that cost might go away beyond what would be the fair value, and away beyond what would be the reasonable and necessary expenditure.
With regard to the Quebec and. Saguenay road, it certainly seems to me extraordinary that the cost of this uncompleted road, because it is very far from completion, should have reached, as suggested by the figures of the Acting Minister of Railways, the enormous sum of something like $80,000 per mile, That cost is certainly very large, and the figures are somewhat startling, because the road is not there; the report of the engineer

says that the road is in a very bad condition, and would require the expenditure of a considerable sum of money to bring the work which has been done up to what it was before work ceased in 1911 or 1912. I would therefore urge this upon the Minister of Railways, and I do so from no desire in any way to obstruct or delay the passage of the Bill. I know nothing at all as to the merits of these roads, and, as I stated yesterday, I do not desire to interpose any objection to their acquisition; but as to the mode in which the judge of the Exchequer Court shall determine the amount to be paid, I think that if the minister sees an objection to the judge fixing the value in the ordinary way, which would enable him to determine the value of this road upon a just and equitable basis,-if there are difficulties standing in the way of that, I think the judge should be required to fix the amount at what, in his judgment, was the actual, reasonable and necessary cost of the road so far as constructed. If that course is adopted, Parliament will simply be following the principle which it has laid down in the Acts relating to the granting of increased subsidies for railroads in which case the extra amount can only be given upon determination by the minister, from the report of his chief engineer, of what has been the acutal, reasonable and necessary cost of the construction of the road. That would be following the principle which was laid down years ago, and upon which Parliament and the Government have been acting ever since.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Before answering the hon.
member, I wish to correct the impression he has with reference to the Bill which I submitted to the House, and which was passed, relating to the Exchequer Court. The hon. member stated last night that that Bill, having been introduced this session, and late in the session, had the appearance of being introduced by reason of the Government taking over these railways. I may explain for the information of the hon. member why that Bill was introduced this session. The Government was disposing of a small piece of canal property at Sault Ste. Marie.
The price asked by the Government was considered larger than the parties purchasing thought it was worth. They agreed that it should be submitted to Judge Cas-sels of the Exchequer Court and I secured the passage of an Order in Council. Judge Cassels approached me and stated that this was not an Exchequer Court case, that
he would not act as arbitrator, but that if it were within his jurisdiction he would gladly take it up and of course without any cost or remuneration whatever. Acting on his suggestion, and after discussing the matter with the Minister of Justice, I submitted a Bill to extend the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court to take in cases such as the sale of lands by the Government. The Minister of Justice prepared a Bill to cover the matters contained therein. There was no question of this railway at that time.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: The two merely synchronized.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Synchronized, that is true.
However, I am glad the Bill does give the Exchequer Court that jurisdiction because I believe we all have confidence in that court. I have never heard it criticised since I have been a member of this House. With reference to the suggestion of the hon. member, it does seem to me that the amendment which I propose covers about all that the hon. gentleman wishes and safeguards in every way the interests of the Government. As was stated by the Solicitor Gen-er last evening, the judge of the Exchequer Court, no doubt, after reading this Bill wished to have some basis in order to arrive at a proper valuation, and he, without any suggestion from any member of the Government, or any other person as far as I am aware, for it was never discussed with any one in connection with the Exchequer Court, wrote to the Minister of Justice suggesting that some basis be put in the Bill in order that the court might arrive at a proper valuation. The basis in the amendment I am suggesting is this:
Said value to' be the actual cost of said railways less depreciation-
That covers the point of the hon. member. *
-but not to exceed $4,465,000, exclusive of outstanding bonded indebtedness which is to be assumed by the Government, but not to exceed in all $2,500,000.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Is that outside of the
$4,465,000?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Yes. As I said last night, we are purchasing three different railways, one on the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix, for $2,500,000. That includes the terminals at Quebec which, I am informed, represent a very large sum of money, which has been placed at $1,000,000 or $2,000,000.

They are located in Quebec city and they are a very valuable asset in connection with this railway. This railway represents $2,500,000 and we assume these bonds. The $4,135,000 is the maximum price that we have to pay the Quebec and Saguenay in case the Exchequer Court comes to the conclusion that that amount has actually been expended.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Do the Canadian Pacific get any of these terminals?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: No, they do not.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Have they got any?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I could not say, I am sure. I do not know. Perhaps I could find that out and let the hon. gentleman know. The $4,135,000 will be paid for the Quebec and Saguenay railway and $330,000 for the Lot-biniere and Megantic. The proprietors of the Quebec and Saguenay must show that $4,135,000 have been actually expended on this railway and they must show that that expenditure has been in cash. They tell me that the books of the company have been audited by Messrs. P. 8. Ross & Sons, Montreal, and that the audit will show that a much larger amount has been expended on the railway. If the property has been depreciated in any way on account of washouts, or by other causes, it must be put in the condition in which it was at the time this expenditure was made. The Government feel that in taking these roads over in this way, the proprietors must in every case, even in the case of the Quebec and Charlevoix, show that the values are actual and not inflated. For instance, with reference to the Quebec and Charlevoix, they must prove to the satisfaction of the Exchequer Court that they have expended $2,500,000. If they do that we are willing to assume the bonds,

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Is the Government going to take the bonds at par?	.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: We are going to take the $2,500,000 bonds at par.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: What are they quoted at to-day?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I do not know what they are quoted at but these are guaranteed bonds.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: They have been going up within the last month or so on the prospect of handing over this proposition to the Government, but why should the Government pay more than they were worth three months ago?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: There are a good many things that go up on the prospect of things happening 'in this country and they may have gone up the same as anything else. The hon. gentleman knows that on the prospect of tariff changes many things go up. Probably the hon. gentleman has (benefited in that way in the past.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Who gets the tip?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: We cannot help giving a tip when we introduce 'a Bill of this kind. That is the position as far as the Quebec and Charlevoix railway is concerned. They must show that the amount which I have stated has been, actually expended on the Lotbiniere and Megantic railway; otherwise the price will be decreased. We have put in the maximum amount. They tell me that instead of $4,135,000 they will be able to show that the actual amount that has been expended on the Quebec and Saguenay is more than $2,500,000 over and above the subsidies. This railway being in this condition, and the people requiring the service that they are entitled to along that shore, we feel that this railway system should be connected up with, and that it will be an acquisition to the Transcontinental railway. There has been considerable profit on the roads that have been in operation. The Quebec and Saguenay will pay its way in the same way 'as these other roads will. That is the reason why we would like to see this Bill go through and the matter placed in such shape that the people in that part of Canada will have the benefit of a service that they should have had many years ago.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Did the companies give to the minister any explanation of the fact that in October last they offered to give clear title to these roads for $620,000 while in May of this year they ask the amount that is proposed to be paid them and which must have been quite a surprise to the minister? Did they give any explanation of such a very large figure.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The only explanation I got
was that, when I was discussing the matter with them, they said that they had made a mistake in figuring out the amount, and that they had put into the roads about $1,000,000 more than they had stated.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Men must be very rich to make a mistake of that kind.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Mistakes of that kind are
sometimes made. We do not want to pay

any more than has gone into the road, and they must show exactly what that amount is.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Does the minister intend to pay for promotion expenses? I understand that these three companies have had a stock-jobbing career for some years, and that their promotion expenses are very great.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I have already stated that we ' only proposed to pay the amount that has actually been spent on the construction of the road. That will not include any promotion expenses whatever; it will include nothing outside of what has actually gone into the road, and the Judge of the Exchequer Court will decide what amount that is.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Why does the minister dispense with the usual requirement that the certificate of the General Manager of the Intercolonial shall he obtained before any branches are taken over?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
It has been the custom to obtain the certificate of the General Manager and his engineers in the case of roads that have been completed and are in operation. But this is a road that has not been completed. If we were to get the General Manager to make a valuation it would probably not 'be as satisfactory as an independent valuation would be, made by the Judge of the Exchequer Court.
'Mr. GRAHAM: That is not what the General Manager was to do. He was to recommend to the Government that the purchase of a certain road would be in the interest of the public and of the road of which it was to become a branch. My opinion is that the General Manager will not do anything of the kind with regard to these particular roads, and he is right. I am not going to waste any time discussing these propositions. They are indefensible from beginning to end, from every point of view, and it is no use going into details. I know, and the Government knows I know, a great deal about these roads, and I make the statement that their purchase in the heyday of prosperity, when we had an overflowing treasury, would be very questionable. But to-day, in the face of out present fihancial condition, when every man is bearing all he can in the way of taxation, the purchase is nothing short of monstrous to my mind. The road on the south side, exclusive of the line from
Quebec to Ste. Anne de Beaupre, is the best of the lot. The line from Quebec to Ste. Anne de Beaupre is run by electricity, and is all right. My judgment is that the line on the south side is a better purchase than either of the otheT roads that are being purchased on the north side; and yet when I was minister I refused to consider the purchase of this road as a branch line of the Intercolonial. It was owned by a very warm personal friend, but I did not think the purchase could be justified. I am not going to. discuss this any further, as I have now made my protest. At this time, when our finances are in such a condition that the Finance Minister has to impose special taxation on the country for war purposes, it seems to me nothing less than an outrage on the business enterprise of Canada and on our taxpayers to take part of the money that the industries of Canada are paying in taxes to put into these schemes. My hon. friend knows that, although only $4,000,000 is mentioned here, he is really committing the country to an expenditure of more than $10,000,000; and that is a small estimate of the amount that will be required to meet the liabilities incurred in the purchase of rolling stock and the completion of these roads, and getting them into running shape. The minister does not expect that the line is going to pay, but I am not going to discuss that side of it, because there are some districts that should be supplied with railway facilities even when we do not expect to make any money out of them; I have always taken that ground, and I do still. But at this particular time, when we do not know what out financial condition will 'be in the future, and when financial conditions are so strenuous for all the people of Canada, it is unspeakable that the Government should ask this Parliament to commit the country to an expenditure of more than $10,000,000.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
There is one point to
which I should like to direct the minister's attention. In this estimate, which is to tie the hands of the judge of the Exchequer Court-there is no getting over that-and which is to convey to him the opinion of this Parliament that he can safely adopt, the figures mentioned in the amendment of my hon. friend, the amount that is to be assumed by the Government is put at $2,500,000; that is, to provide for the bonds on the electric road. And yet in this very report which has been brought down to Parliament, the total cost of replacing that electric railway is put at $1,115,200.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I think the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has not quite the correct basis in his mind when he makes his criticism. The duty of the Exchequer Court, under the Act as now before the House, would be, not to assume that the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix road was worth $2,500,000, because these bonds were against it, which we must assume, and then pass on to the other roads and value them. On the contrary, the principle is this: the Exchequer Court will take one road at a time and ascertain the cost of that road, irrespective entirely of what may be against the road.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Why not take the value?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I will come to that
again if the hon. gentleman desires. Having dealt in this way with the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix road, the court would then come to the Quebec and Saguenay and find the actual money which has been invested there-not the money that may have been paid out by the company, but the money that has found its way into the property. The same would be done with respect to the Megantic and Lotbiniere road. The three would be added to ascertain the grand total. From this would be deducted the $2,500,000 bonds which must be left against the entire property though in fact it rests only against the first property. Then, if the balance should exceed the figure allowed, the balance would be reduced to that figure. If, on the contrary, the balance should be be-

low the maxi mum figure, that balance alone is what the country would pay. There is not in the Bill the slightest intimation to the judge of the Exchequer Court that he would be safe in allowing $4,465,000. If the net cost is less than that amount after deducting $2,500,000, that net cost is all that can possibly be charged against the country for the total purchase. It is argued -by one hon. gentleman, the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver)-that whatever might be the claims of this locality in ordinary times, those claims should not be heard because of the strained financial conditions of the present time. I cannot but recognize that there is some force in that contention, and only unusually great necessities should impel us at this time to the taking over of these properties by the Government. But there is greater necessity than could be pointed out in any other part of the country, by one cardinal consideration to which I am about to refer. As regards two of the roads: the Montmorency and Charlevoix and the Lotbinifere and Megantic, I do not think there can be any doubt that, from the point of view of earning power, as a good business purchase, they are very desirable for the country to acquire. Their earning power in the past has been given, and one of them particularly is of value to the Intercolonial. It has been admitted by the hon. member for St. John that the criticism that has been offered could not be applied to Uiese roads, and the same is admitted by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). While I am on the subject of these two roads, I might state that as to them the basis of valuation that is offered to the Exchequer Court in this Bill is very decidedly to the advantage of the country, because it would seem to me that probably a much higher figure would be allowed on the ordinary legal basis of value upon which the Exchequer Court rests its verdicts. However, the extraordinary feature to which I have referred comes when we consider the Quebec and Saguenay. Here is a road in which a great deal of money was invested. It was subsidized by the Government of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in 1910, and so had the sanction of that Administration. It is a road that was necessary for the service of the district into which it was to extend. As the result of the assistance given by the Government of Quebec, by the former Dominion Government as well as by this Government in 1912, very 253
considerable progress was made and very considerable moneys were expended.
The road was built from Cap Tourmente right on to Murray Bay so far as acquiring the right of way and the building of the actual roadbed was concerned. Dikes were built along the river St. Lawrence to protect the structure from- the inroads of the river; indeed, from Murray Bay to Nairn Falls the road was completed and is now in actual operation and carrying traffic. May I mention in passing, for fear I forget it, that the first road mentioned in the Bill, the Montmorency and Charlevoix, carried last year, my information is, no fewer than 1,800,000 passengers. Such, then, is the work that was done in connection with this Quebec and Saguenay line.

What js the average
fare?

speechtext: Not for passengers.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: What kind of operation is it?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I really could not
answer that. There are pulp mills at Nairn Falls and it serves them.

speechtext: What is the production of those mills?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.

I cannot give the
figures, but they can be given in the course of this discussion in committee.

I understood that Nairn
Falls was the terminus of the Quebec and Saguenay?

I understood that the

speechtext:
But not for passenger
business.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The committee is to be congratulated upon having heard from a member of the Government the Govern-

merit's justification for the proposals now under consideration, looked at from a national standpoint. We heard from the Postmaster General yesterday a justification of the proposals from the .standpoint of the people of the locality affected. That was natural, right and proper; every one could understand and appreciate the standpoint of the Postmaster General and of those for whom he spoke. But when the Solicitor General undertakes to justify the proposal upon national grounds on identically the same basis as the reasons given by the Postmaster General, I cannot agree that the grounds offered by him furnish any justification whatever for the proposals; rather do I say that those grounds condemn them absolutely. There are 30,000 people, he says, who need railway communication. As I stated yesterday I can find him many places throughout this Dominion of Canada where 30,000 people need railway accommodation just as much as do the people along the route of this railroad. Nay, I can find people who need it ten times, a thousand times more. The people along the route of this road, during half the year at any rate, have the advantage of the navigation of the St. Lawrence, which certainly can take any product that they have to sell or bring to their doors any requirement that they may have to buy, and do it just as cheaply and just as	readily as any railroad will.
I will admit that it would be desirable that these people should have a railroad, and, no doubt, if the circumstances were favourable, they would have one. No doubt aid m behalf of such a railroad was warranted at the time1 it was given; but, the conditions being as they are, I am afraid we shall have to suggest that the money !has not always been wisely expended. The fact is that the' people have not a railroad, and the people of Canada are called upon to give them a railroad. As I have said, equal numbers of people, in tens, or dozens, or hundreds of other localities throughout the country, are in just as great need of a railroad, and could be supplied with railroad facilities for very much less money. How much is this sixty-two miles of railway going to cost the Dominion of Canada? We are buying forty-two miles of the Quebec, Charlevoix and Montmorency railway, and some thirty miles of the Megan tic railway. Whether we buy those railroads or not, the people and the interests served by their existence and operation will continue to be served in 253i
the same way. The people along those two sections covered 'by the proposal now before the House are not in the same position as the people along the line of the Quebec and Saguenay railway. The plea made by the Solicitor General, the plea upon which the Government rests its demand upon Parliament for this sum of money, is based upon the requirements of the people living along the sixty odd miles of the Quebec and Saguenay. It cannot be based upon the requirements of the people living along the Quebec, Charlevoix and Montmorency, or upon the claims of the people living alorfg the Megantic railway, because those railways are in existence and in operation. Therefore, taking the Solicitor General's own argument as it has been presented to the House, we are paying out the amount of money that we are called upon to pay for the benefit of the people living along the sixty odd miles of the uncompleted Quebec and Saguenay railway. The ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) says that the total amount will be in the neighbourhood of $10,000,000; and, as nearly as I can figure, that $10,000,000, if considered as being the expenditure necessary to afford railway accommodation to the people living along the Quebec and Saguenay railway, comes to about $130,000 a mile that this country is being called upon to pay in order that these 30,000 people who are living along that sixty-one miles of. railroad shall have railroad accommodation in addition to the water transportation which they have now.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
places the figures at about double what they should be.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I am saying that it comes to $130,000 a mile if we consider the whole expenditure as being made necessary in order to afford accommodation to the people along this 61 miles.
My hon. friend made a plea as between conditions in the West and in the East. I happen to have knowledge of a locality, not in my own but in the adjoining constituency, where a larger population than that along the line of the Quebec and Saguenay, a population having no river navigation to aid them, are living at a distance, not of 10 miles, 15 miles, 20 miles, or 30 miles, or 40 miles from a railroad, but living at a distance of from 60 to 120 miles from the nearest railroad. I have brought the condition of these people before this Parliament on a previous occasion.

Their position is that the Provincial Government guaranteed aid to a line of railroad to be built for their relief. That line is in an uncompleted condition, just as is the Quebec and Saguenay; but this Government has seen fit to take that piece of road as a part of the property on which it holds security against the Canadian Northern Railway.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Is the road uncompleted In the same sense as the Quebec and Saguenay? Is it not completed as far as it goes?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: It is in the same position as the Quebec and Saguenay; it is graded, but there are no rails.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: What is the line?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: It is the St. Paul de Metis branch of the Canadian Northern Railway.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The same condition
exists in Saskatchewan in two or three cases.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The population of which I speak are largely French-speaking, just as are the people below the city of Quebec. This railroad is taken by the Government as a part of the property upon which it holds security against the Canadian Northern company for the guarantee given two years ago. In the proposals which the Government have placed before the House for a loan to the Canadian Northern railway, they have included money to pay the interest on the bonds issued by the company, guaranteed by the province, for the construction and completion of that road. When the matter was brought to the attention of the Government, my friend the Solicitor General said that the amount realized from the sale of bonds was not sufficient to complete, and that additional money would be necessary in order to complete. In my judgment it would be business on the part of the country to find the money to complete in order that that railroad should earn the interest on its bonds, instead of the interest being paid out of the Treasury on an uncompleted road. In addition to that, the people would get the benefit of facilities for traffic, and the country would be developed because of those facilities. But the Minister of Finance said that that was not possible-that they had gone as far as they could in appropriating money for the aid of railroads at this session, and that he could not reconsider the Government's position or consider the claims of this particular railroad and of 
the people whose rights and interests depend upon its completion. There is another railroad in my own constituency, the Peace river branch of the Canadian Northern railway, which is graded for about 100 miles, and on which about 30 miles of track has been laid. The trains are in operation on that portion of 30 miles, and for the balance, of something over 50 miles the grading has been completed, but there are no rails. This grading was completed, I think three years ago, and the condition is absolutely identical with that of the Quebec and Saguenay. The grading, trestles, etc., are being damaged or destroyed by the weather.
I brought that case to the attention of the Acting Minister of Railways and the answer 'he gave was that he could do nothing, that there was no money available to supplement the aid that it was proposed to give to the Canadian Northern, and that would enable these roads to be completed.
I did not ask for it in the interests of the Canadian Northern; I asked for it on the one hand, in the interests of the people whom I represent, and who need facilities for the traffic which these roads would give if they were completed, and on the other in the interests of the country, which to-day is paying interest on bonds on roads which by reason of not being completed are not able to earn interest on these bonds, and which, if completed, would earn interest. Under these circumstances, it strikes me, as it must strike a great many other people, anything but favourably that $130,000 should be taken to supplement what has been done already in the way of giving aid for the completion of this railroad, while these other railroads, and the people who are dependent upon them, receive no consideration whatever.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Along the road to which the hon. gentleman refers, are there any towns say of 2,000 or 3,000 population, any settled conditions such as there are in the area of the railways under consideration?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: What towns are they?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon, I thought he meant settlements. There are no towns such as there are at Murray Bay.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Then the position is
different.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The position is different and very much worse, because ours is a

rural population producing from the land, who, unless given railway communication, cannot produce, and cannot live there and do any good. It is a question of the progress of the country, of the development which we ail talk about, of our immigration policy, and of the necessity of settlement. Instead of spending our money to redeem the conditions as they exist there, we are going to spend $10,000,000 upon a project in regard to which we have no obligations, and which certainly is not going to produce results in proportion to the amount of money expended. In a time like this, we have to consider that.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I take it from the hon. gentleman's argument that if the times had been propitious he thinks that these roads should be built in 'both places, in the West and also in this portion of Quebec, to give relief to the people.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
If we had plenty of money, I would not object at all, everything else being proper. But if we are short of money where a great necessity exists, we seem to have abundance of money where the lesser necessity exists, and I cannot recognize that as a sound principle, or one that I can support.
Since my hon. friend has projected a certain idea into this discussion very delicately and very cleverly, that is to say, the suggestion of a divergence of interests between the East and the West, let me say that in the matter of railway transportation there is not only no divergence of interests, but there is an absolute inter-dependence of interests. The development of the West demands railroad facilities in the East just as the development of the West is necessary to make the railroads in the East of advantage. We are proposing to spend $10,000,000 on 61 miles of railway, because that is what it amounts to, so faT as national benefit is concerned. I admit the private benefit to [DOT] the gentlemen who own these enterprises, which while they earn more than will pay the cost of operation, do not earn enough, I understand from the statement of the Acting Minister of Railways, to pay interest on the cost of construction. I believe that is correct, that the Quebec, Charlevoix and Chicoutimi railway while it earns more than enough to pay its operating expenses does not earn enough to pay interest on the capital cost as well.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: My information is that it does.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: If it does, we are not in any way called upon to spend any money upon it.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Except that the other road cannot 'be operated without it; the other road would be isolated. It is for our advantage that we are taking the Quebec and Charlevoix railway. I do not see how my hon. friend can add that to the country's burden..

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: That proves exactly what I was saying, that the burden of the country is in respect of the sixty-one miles of the Quebec and Saguenay railway. That is the 'burden upon the country. If we have $10,000,000 to spend on railway development, and we want to spend it in eastern Canada, I would make a suggestion to the minister-I have had occasion to make it before, and I shall make it again-by which we could spend that money in a way that would produce enormous results to the city of Quebec, and to every interest that depends on the city of Quebec, and that would be of enormous benefit to western 'Canada as well. When we were discussing this matter before the Acting Minister of Railways intimated, as the Minister of Finance had intimated, that only the limitations of finance prevented his dealing with the problem as I presented it. Quebec is the great Atlantic deep water ocean port of Canada. Quebec is the Atlantic summer terminus of the Transcontinental road. Quebec has advantages as a port which no other city in the Dominion of Canada has. We have built a railroad from Winnipeg to Quebec, at a cost of nearly $200,000,000, for t'he purpose of handling traffic through the elevators at that city, and we did not handle it there during the past winter. Although we have the traffic, although it needs to find its outlet at Quebec, we are not handling it there, partly because we have not the equipment on the railroad, but, more than anything else, because we have not elevator accommodation at the city of Quebec. The success of the Transcontinental railway enterprise depends upon the establishment at the port of Quebec of adequate elevator accommodation more than upon any other consideration. We have there an elevator carrying 1,500,000 bushels.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Has it been filled?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
It- has not been filled. Will my hon. friend suggest that it was not

filled because we had not the grain to fill it with?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: They would not ship it there.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: My hon. friend told us that he had not the oars to haul the grain with, and, if he had had the cars and had hauled the grain there he would not have had any place in which to put it, because they have not the elevators. When I asked why lhe was not providing greater elevator accommodation at Quebec he said it was because the Government could not afford the money, but it can afford the money to relieve our friends in regard to this uncompleted sixty-one miles of Quebec and Saguenay railway. It can do that, but it cannot afford the money to build elevators at the city of Quebec, which would make Quebec the great ocean port of this Dominion during seven months of every year, which it cannot be unless that elevator accommodation is provided there and provided on a scale similar to that which now exists at the head of lake Superior.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman say that any grain was offered for transcontinental shipment that had to be refused for lack of equipment, or that any grain was offered for the elevator at Quebec for which there was not room?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I do not know.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
All the grain offered
was shipped on the Transcontinental railway, and there has been room in the elevator at Quebec.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I do not know anything
about that, but I do know that in several cases in the Prairie West railway companies refused to take grain from the farmers and from the elevators, I presume, because they did not have the facilities to send it east.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: It was not through our lack.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
It was not through the
lack of hon. gentlemen opposite? They are in control of the affairs of this country at the present time.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Not of the railways?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Of the Transcontinental railway and the elevator at Quebec, and if that condition exists my hon. friend may find any reason he pleases for it; but on this Government must rest the responsibility, and when they come and ask this House to pay $10,000,000 for 61 miles of uncom-

pleted railway to accommodate 30,000 people, I ask them how they can expect us to vote that money without a protest, when the money is so urgently needed to establish elevator accommodation at Quebec, so that the $200,000,000 sunk in the Transcontinental railway may earn interest and so that the people of the prairies, upon whose industry and success depend the earnings of the Transcontinental railway and the development of the city of Quebec, shall be able to progress and develop as they must, or else the whole enterprise falls to the ground. They are in control and, instead of them spending the money of this country in establishing at that port these facilities that will enable it to do the trade of the country, they take untold amounts of money, spend them for other purposes, and refuse these facilities to the port of Quebec. My hon. friends do not seem to like Quebec for some reason, because, while they had a road from Quebec to Winnipeg completed, they did not see fit to give a service on that road last winter. They gave a service from Toronto to Winnipeg over roads that did not belong to them for 500 miles, where they competed with the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific-a very good thing for Toronto, but not a very good thing for Quebec, when every reason suggested that they should put on a service between Quebec and Winnipeg.
If they do not like Quebec, if they propose to put it on the side track, if they propose that that great ocean port of Canada shall be ignored in their policy, notwithstanding the fact that $200,000,000 has been spent on the railway to bring the business to that port, we havte another port -the port of Montreal. We have a railway which is proposing to establish terminals in the city of Montreal. The Canadian Northern has a line uncompleted from Montreal to Capreol. Unless and: until that line is completed to Montreal, with suitable terminals in Montreal, the Canadian Northern railway system cannot be a successful enterprise. No matter who is at the head of the enterprise, no ^natter what shall happen, unless and until it secures terminals and facilities to enable the trade to reach Montreal over a completed line, it cannot be a success. I mentioned the matter to the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) when the Canadian Northern Bill was up. The answer was that there was not enough money; we could not take that matter into consideration; we

could loan the Canadian Northern $15,000,000, but we could not do anything to see that the money was spent so that the railway would be a completed enterprise, and, to that degree, able to earn interest on its cost. So that, for the ports of Quebec and Montreal, for the vast interests that centre in each of these great cities, for the transportation interests that are involved in the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern, and for the great interests that are behind them in the prairie West, dependent on these railways and upon their access to these ocean ports, there is no consideration at the hands of the Government, but 30,000 people along the shores of the St. Lawrence, where they have navigation during seven months in the year, cowering a distance of sixty-one miles, are to have the benefit of an expenditure of $10,000,000 by this Government. We are to be saddled with $500,000 a year interest by reason of the proposition that our friends put before the House to-day. But we cannot get elevator accommodation at the port of Quebec, and we cannot assist the Canadian Northern into Montreal more than we have assisted it. We are able to pay interest on the bonds of the branch lines in the prairie West, guaranteed by the provincial governments, in order to hold our securities, but we are not able to complete the lines so that the people there will get the same facilities as we are offering to these people below Quebec at this cost. My hon. friend the Solicitor General, I presume, has made the best plea that he can on behalf of the Government for the expenditure that they propose to make, but it is not a plea that appeals to my mind as being in the national interest.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Yesterday the hon. acting Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid) gave the capitalization of the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix railway at about $3,000,000 and he gave the earnings for 1914 as being $83,000, for 1913, $76,000 and for the years before that about the same. The Solicitor General says that that pays.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: On the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I would much rather
have my hon. friend for my law partner
than for my business partner if he thinks that that pays on $3,000,000 of capital stock.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I did not say that it
paid on the capital stock.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: You said that to my hon. friend.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
My information was
that it paid the interest on the bonds.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend asked
that question, and you said that you thought it paid the interest on the capital stock.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: No, I did not say that. What he asked about were the fixed charges.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
He said the capital
*stock.	.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I do not think he will say that himself.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I think I did, but I am
not sure I meant it in the sense in which my hon. friend (Mr. Nesbitt) does.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I still say that if the
Solicitor General says that is a paying road, I would rather he put money into it than that I should. We come next to the Lot-biniere and Megantic. Last year they made the enormous profit of $1,255 with a capitalization of $349,000. There is nothing in this return to show how much money was spent on repairs or maintenance. In this return there is an engineer's report showing that improvements and repairs must be made upon the road. I notice in one case that 6,000 feet of filling has to be done. Everybody knows that a railway or any other enterprise depends entirely on how you keep up the property. On maintenance depends whether you make any net profits out of it or not.
If you starve the road for the purpose of showing a net profit, you may get the net profit all right, but very much to the detriment of the road. My hon. friend thinks that as there are 30,000 people in that district, the road might pay. Now it is estimated by the best American railway statisticians that it takes 2,000 people to the mile to make a railway pay.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I do not think I made any statement as to whether the road would pay; I do not think I am competent to judge.	,

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
How can a road with
only 500 people to the mile pay?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: The hon. member knows that besides population bringing railroads, railroads bring population.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: It depends on the country. You cannot dig rocks and grow wheat.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I have done it.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: You did not make much at it. It would be much better for you to let the farmer dig the rocks and you advise him as to the law. I absolutely agree with my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) that there is no human excuse for taking over these roads nor foT building that new piece. The Lotbiniere and Megantic railway already has connection with the Intercolonial and the Grand Trunk, and can therefore already feed the Intercolonial, if that is what the minister wants. The road could not 'be better located, so far as connection with other roads is concerned. There is no earthly excuse for taking over these roads or for building that new piece. There is not even the excuse that this road has a Dominion charter, for it got its charter from the Quebec legislature. We have always been opposed to interfering with provincial rights, and now we have the opportunity of putting our theory into practice. If it is necessary that this road should be built, let the province of Quebec build it by all means, but I do not think we should build it, or take over this other little piece of road. It is an imposition on the people of Canada to ask them to do it at this time of financial strain and stress, and I do not believe there is a man in the Government although they are defending this proposition, and putting it through, who really thinks in his own heart that the road should be taken over. For my part, I want to raise my voice in opposition to the Government's spending one dollar on this proposition this year; we cannot afford to do it in any shape, manner, or form. There is no possible way of showing that any of these roads will pay; they never have paid in the past, as their reports show.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I understand that while the Lotbiniere and Megantic railway did not pay last year for some reason connected with the management; in previous years it paid a very good return.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The net earnings in 1913 were $6,905, and" in 1912 $5,577, on a capitalization of $349,000. As I said a moment ago, we do not know how the maintenance of the road has suffered through the net earnings. If there is anything to earn in that district the road should have earned it before this time, and I have no doubt it has been in operation for some years.

As far as I am concerned, I am absolutely opposed to the Government spending one dollar on these roads this year.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Knowing
something about this road and the district through which it runs, perhaps I might say a few words. The Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix railway runs from St. Paul street, in the city of Quebec, to Cap Tourmente, a distance of about thirty miles. Part of the road is double-tracked, eighty-pound rails being used. There is no' better roadbed in the Dominion. Last year this road carried 1,843,000 passengers, but the average fare was about 124 cents, due to the short haul. A great number of pilgrims come every year to the shrine of Ste. Anne de Beaupre, coming over the American lines, over the Canadian Pacific railway, the Quebec Central, and so on. These roads get the biggest percentage of the fare, and we get about forty cents per passenger. This road runs through a thickly populated district, and the right-of-way is very expensive. The hon. member for St. John said a moment ago that the engineers had estimated the cost of this road at $1,300,000. I do not think that figure took into account the right-of-way and the rolling stock.
Mr. PUGSLEY- They are both included.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I have the
statement here. There are 22 stations on this 30 miles of road. The station and other buildings-I am not taking into account the land-cost $134,000, and they could not be replaced for that amount to-day.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: What are the names of the stations?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Quebec, Limoi-lou Junction, Maizerets, Park Maufils, de-Salabery, Monument, Beauport, Everell, St. Gregoire, Montmorency Falls, Boischatel, Riviere de Fer, L'Ange Gardien Station,. Petit Pre', Lemoine, Laverdiere, Chateau Richer, Visitation, Riviere Aux Chiens, Ste. Anne de Beaupre, Beaupre, St. Joachim. The rolling stock and the stations and other buildings are worth $409,000. The terminus at the city of Quebec comprises about 135,000 feet of land and is worth nearer $2,000,000 than $1,500,000. If you put it at $10 a foot, it would be worth $1,350,000. The Government has already taken over about 40 per cent of these terminals.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: At what cost?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The Canadian Pacific railway contributed their lands at $12 a foot. The reason why this land had to be taken over in this way was that the Canadian Pacific railway had not sufficient room for the Union station and freight shed, and also our railway stood between their tracks and the St. Lawrence basin, where their Empresses dock. The Canadian Pacific railway, of course, could not expropriate our railway, so the Government took it over and then turned it over to the Canadian Pacific railway. Our road is double tracked part of the way, making the total mileage 43 miles. The cotton company at Montmorency does not benefit this road very much, as the haul is short, and the freight is turned over to the Canadian Northern railway or tne Canadian Pacific railway; but when the Government acquires this road the freight will be turned over to the Intercolonial railway. The Saguenay railway was incorporated in 1905 at the request of my Liberal friends of Quebec; I may say that they are nearly all Liberals in Quebec city. The incorporators were: Hon. E. B. Garneau, Hon. Charles Langelier, George Tanguay, M.P.P., Narcisse Rioux, Hon. Alex. Taschereau, William Price,
Mark Workman,'McLeaWalbank.W. G. Ross,
They tried to raise the capital in 1907, but did not succeed, owing to the financial crisis. In 1909, being encouraged by the late Government, who gave us the subsidies, and encouraged also by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), who said he would do all he could for me, but advised me to see the Prime Minister, now leader of the Opposition, we started work in 1911. Work was stopped in 1912-not 1911, as stated by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) last night.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: It was the Acting Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) who said that; I only quoted his words.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
No, I said it commenced in
1911, and that work was suspended in 1912.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
No, he said the work
stopped in September, 1911.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Hansard will show what I
said.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Work was
stopped in 1912. About 87 per cent of the road is completed; the ties, fishplates and spikes are all along the road, and part of the rails. There is a population there that has been waiting for railway communication a little longer than some of the west- . ern population of which the hon. member for Edmonton spoke-these people having been waiting for 150 years for transportation facilities. They have paid their taxes for the development of the railways of the West. They do not begrudge that; but we think that they now are entitled to means of transportation. From the- 10th of November to the 10th of May in each year, the people are absolutely cut off from civilization. There are no roads-nothing that can be properly called roads-through those mountains. There are severe frosts, extending to 45 degrees below zero, and so transportation by road is almost impossible. The late Government in 1904 established a ferry between Riviere Ouelle	and	Murray	Bay,	fromthe south to	the	north	shore,	andbuilt a line	nine	miles	long	fromRivifere Ouelle	junction to	the wharf.
That service cost l-ast year, as shown by the Department of Marine and Fisheries, $53,240.66. This amount can be saved by the completion of the Saguenay railway. The transportation of mail Costs $6,918.69, by railway, boat and team, of which the railway gets $1,500-that is, from Quebec to St. Joachim. The maintenance of the branch from Riviere Ouelle junction to the wharf, according to the Railway Department, cost about $22,000. These sums make a total of $82,159. The earnings of the Montmorency railway are $83,031 above expenses, and of the Lotbiniere and Megantic, $3,889. These are all actual figures. The only estimate of earnings is of the Saguenay railway, which is estimated -by Mr. E. Evans engineer, of Quebec, at $315,511. These earnings, actual and estimated, together with the savings, make a total of $484,590. Take from this the steamer Champlain's earnings of last year, $7,093.90. The balance would represent about 5 per cent 0-n $9,000,000 of capital. So these roads would not be by any means a "white elephant' far from it. In my opinion, as soon as the Quebec and Saguenay is completed,.the Government should have at least 5 per cent on its investment, which would not be ten millions, nor would it be nine millions, but would be closer to seven millions than eight millions. My hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) said last night that he at one time lived about one hundred miles east of Murray Bay,-I do not know whether on the south shore or on the north shore,-and he could not believe in a winter port on the St. Lawrence. I would advise him to read the report made on the winter port of St. Catherines bay by Ad-

miral Bayfield in 1882, by engineer J. C. Tache in 1904, and by Edward Evans in 1912; also the report of the commission for exploring the Saguenay in 1829; notes on the Saguenay country in 1829 by Andrew Stuart and by Lieut. Baddeley and Commissioner Ollebar in 1860, and also by the former Deputy Minister of Public Works, Mr. Gobeil, who gave a conference in the city of Quebec; and also a report of Judge Langelier. He will learn from these documents that even at low tide you have in St. Catherine's bay 71 feet of water. It is shown in Mr. J. C. TachAs report that you	can	take a	steamer to
within 50 feet of the shore of St. Catherine's bay, and you can winter there in open water all winter. I have my summer home at St. Irenee, and I go there in winter when I can. The north shore channel is always free of ice. The prevailing winds in winter are from the north, and the ice piles up on the south shore. That is why the ferry established in 1904 has not given the service to the north shore. Last winter I tried four times to get there, but unsuccessfully. I went from Montreal to Riviere Ouelle, slept two days at the Riviere Ouelle wharf and returned to Montreal, having made a round trip of 592 miles without reaching St. Irenee. The steamer that is now used in this ferry service is quite obsolete. I have here a letter from Mr. Johnston, Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, in which he says:
The usefulness of the boat is pretty nearly gone, and if this department is to continue the service, it will be necessary, without delay, to take steps to provide a suitable boat. It is estimated that a suitable boat will cost, at the present time, no less than ?175,000.
As to the money spent on the road, the sum may look large, but every cent of it has gone into the road. There were no sideshows, no subcontractors, so far as the company was concerned. The contract was given to two contractors. From Cap Tour-mente to Murray Bay was given to M. J. O'Brien, at prices which could not be had to-day, and from Murray Bay to Naim Falls was given to the Bishop Construction Company, which failed while building the road, and the work was completed by M. J. O'Brien. The road is operated today, not for passengers, but for freight. It is paying the expense of maintenance, and something over.
Now, with regard to the Montmorency bonds. These were issued about 18 years ago. I do not know of any of them having changed hands since they were issued. They 
are in the hands of insurance companies, of such men as F. W. Ross, of Quebec, and of wealthy estates in Quebec that have kept them from the beginning. There is no market; they are not listed. There has been no promotion money expended on the Quebec and Saguenay railway. Not one five cent piece has any director received either as fees, or as salary, or even as expenses, either directly or indirectly. I am not interested in the Quebec and Saguenay, the Lotbiniere and Megantic, or the Charlevoix and Montmorency railways.
So far as that error of $3,473,000 as against $4,465,000 is concerned I am the guilty party. When I came back with the Minister of Railways, he asked me to write a letter on this subject. I was in my office, in Montreal, in communication with the controller in Quebec, and he gave me the figures. So, I wrote the letter. When the matter came before the Government, I went to Quebec to check the figures, i I talked the matter over with him, and the only explanation he gave me was that he was under the impression that we were working under a deed of trust which would give a clear title to the Government if 67 per cent of the bonds of the railway were handed over to the Trust Co. and cancelled.
Every one in the city of Quebec, including the Board of Trade and the city council, have asked for this road and believe that the people .are entitled to it. From the 10th of November until the 10th of May the north shore is without service. During the last two yeare they have asked the Government to go to the rescue by sending the steamer Montcalm there to try to help them.
The population of Charlevoix is 22,000, Chicoutimi and Saguenay 65,000, Montmorency 15,000, city of Quebec 90,000, Quebec county 27,000. The city of Quebec will certainly be a feeder of that railway. There is no means of communication below Quebec, because the boat leaves at 8 o'clock in the morning and summer residents wishing to go down there-clerks, merchants, bankers and so on-cannot leave by that boat. If there was a train the whole district would be populated in a comparatively short time. The cost of these railways was $8,921,476.37, of which amount the cost of the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix was $2,992,209.89, and the Lotbiniere and Megantic railway, $349,208.85. This railway was bought from the hon. member

for Richmond and Wolfe (Mr. Tobin) and the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) and we were assured that it earned 5 and 6 per cent all the time. If it is not earning that much it is due to the shortage of cars caused by the Grand Trunk being unable to supply cars to go over this Lotbiniere and Megantic line. I think it is the only branch line which the Intercolonial has not taken over in the province of Quebec. It runs from Lyster in the county of Megantic to 'St. Jean des Chaillons in the county of Lotbiniere. At Lyster it connects with the Grand Trunk railway, at Villeroy with the Intercolonial railway and at Fortierville with the Quebec, Montreal and Southern railway. Surely these people are entitled to some direct railway communication. The member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortier) told me a few days ago that although he lives only thirty miles from the city of Quebec, it takes him two days to get there and back. The Lotbiniere and Megantic railway consists of thirty miles of main line and about two miles of sidings. The county of Megantic has a population of 31,000, and the county of Lotbiniere a population of 22,000. The villages along the lines include Lyster, Lourdes, Villeroy, Kingsbury, Fortierville, Parisville and St. Jean des Chaillons.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: In the engineer's report the total population served by the Lotbiniere and Megantic railway is stated to be only a little ovier 5,000.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I am taking the census and the statement made by the hon. member for Lotbiniere. The census gives the county of Lotbiniere a population of 22,000.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: In his report, the engineer mentions the villages referred to by my hon. friend, and gives the total population as 5,220.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
There may be some villages back from the railway which have escaped the engineer's notice. As to the possibilities of the Quebec and Saguenay railway, I may say that it is not very encouraging for people to try to develop industries in the district when they have communication for only six months in the year. The Mount Mur-4 p.m. ray Pulp and Paper Mill Company, which is controlled exclusively by the New York World, was established in that district. They havie bought, during the last four years, in the
county of Charlevoix, timber lands for which they have paid over $600,000. For the last three years they have produced over 150,000 cords of pulpwood each year, but have been unable to get a cord of it	out owing to	the
lack of railway facilities and narbour accommodation. They proceeded to spend their own money in making the necessary improvements, and this year they will be able to get out some.
