The Baie St. Paul Lumber Company, which is controlled by some Americans from Syracuse, New York, obtained from the seminary of Quebec certain timber rights in that district, for which they paid $280,000. They have spent a .large sum of money there, but they have been discouraged because of the lack of transportation facilities. They can get schooners, but they cannot get steamers, because the water is not deep enough in the bay.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Can they not get ordinary schooners to carry their pulpwood?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: It would take schooners a long time to carry out 60,000 cords of pulpwood. Besides, they do not navigate in winter.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: They can use teams in winter.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I wish my hon. friend would come down to that district with me in the winter, and see the conditions.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: All the way along the St. Lawrence there are scores of big ships that carry timber, sawn timber, and deals all the way from Metis to Riviere du Loup. These vessels do not go into the harbours; they anchor a mile or two outside and are loaded by barges.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
You are
talking of the south shore, where they have the Intercolonial railway wharves, and all that they want in that line. On the north shore the only wharf at which there is water deep enough to accommodate a steamer is at Murray Bay. There is an iron mine in the county of Charlevoix in which at least $250,000 must have been sunk. I know that some of our Quebec friends are only waiting for the construction of this railway before commencing to exploit that mine.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I could tell the hon. gentleman about a lot of mines in which

more money than that was sunk, and in which I myself put some money.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: The man in charge of the Quebec and Saguenay construction was the engineer, Arthur Bruce. The estimates w^re based on reports by Edward Evans and Beresford Fox, of Sir Douglas Fox and partners, of London. Other engineers engaged in the work were J. G. Guay, S. A. Demeules, and E. S. Lovelace. They were absolutely wrong in their estimates, which were just as bad as the estimates of the cost of the Transcontinental. The railway is absolutely level; there are no grades and the roadbed is largely solid rook. I would call the attention of the committee to the terminals which it is necessary for the Transcontinental to have at Quebec. Without terminals you cannot run a railroad, and the same may be said of the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix and the Quebec and Saguenay railroads.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: How will this railway benefit the population of Chicoutimi and Saguenay?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: It will do that when it is taken down to St. Catherine's bay.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: How will this railway benefit the county of Megantic? If the railway is projected through Sherbrooke it will assist the county of Megantic; otherwise it will be of no value to that county.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I am simply taking the statement o| the hon. member for Lotmniere.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I asked if the bonds
would be paid at par by the Government. He said, " Yes." Does he mean the bonds of the Quebec and Montmorency and the bonds of the Quebec and Saguenay?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: What bonds?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: We take the road clear of all encumbrance, and the $2,500,000 of bonds are the original bonds, ae stated by the hon. member from Charlebois.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Does that apply to the two sections?
Mr. M'EIGHEN: No, just the one section.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The object of my question is that I understand that the Quebec and Saguenay has been built; the eurvey-

ing, the locating of the line and the grading, has been done with money invested by the French people. I understand that this money was obtained on the Paris market to the extent of something over $4,000,000. Is that right?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Oh, yes, more than that.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I do not think that any Canadian money was invested in that section from St. Joachim to Nairn Falls, and Surely the people who have invested their money, with whose savings you have built the road, are entitled to reimbursement if the Government are going to absorb it. Personally I am not opposed to the Government taking over that section of the railroad which runs from St. Joachim to Murray Bay. I wish to explain, however, that the Quebec, Lotbiniere and Megantic should not be taken over by the Government. This road was built some years ago by some very enterprising lumbermen for the purpose of exploiting their timber limits. In 1902, if I mistake not, it was bought by Messrs. Tobin, McRae and Pennington for $235,000. This included 60,000 acres of timber land. A few years afterwards, when the limits, had been practically exhausted, the road was sold to the Quebec Eastern for $285,000. As was stated a moment ago by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), the road is connected with the Intercolonial. It is not a highly paying concern, but still it pays its way. I do not see why, in these days of hard times, when the people of Canada are called upon to pay such heavy taxation as they will this year, they should be asked to saddle themselves with this railway, especially when we are told by the Minister of Railways and by the Minister of Finance that the Transcontinental railway, to which this Toad is going to be added, is already a dead weight on the Government. I may be told, it is true, that I should be perhaps more provincial; and that as it is a matter which concerns my own province I should keep silent and let the Government acquire this railroad. My answer is that 'I am elected to the Parliament of Canada not to represent one county or one province, but to represent the people of Canada; and I care not what may be said about the advantage which might accrue to a special locality by the gift of a railway, or rather by the acquiring by the Government of a certain railway. The people of Canada at the present moment are not in a mood

to pay any such amount ot money as this. The war will cost this country an enormous amount of money. The national debt is increasing by leaps and bounds. The people will pay it cheerfully because the people understand that the war must be ended and ended victoriously and that all legitimate sacrifice must be made towards securing that end. Therefore, I think the Government might well ponder and pause before deciding to acquire this small bit of a railroad. As regards the other part of this scheme, that is the railway running from Quebec to St. Joachim. I know that section of the country; it is a rich territory; the railroad runs through alluvial lands, and really I think it is a paying concern. But it is a tramway, and the people are well served as there are twenty-twc or twenty-five stopping places; not stations exactly but stopping places. It is the continuation of the tramway system of the city of Quebec. It pays its way and I think that if it was disconnected from the other stretch of railway which was added to it, the Quebec and Saguenay, there would be no need of acquiring it. Therefore I say that there is no reason for the Goverment acquiring the Quebec and Lotbiniere section of the railway. There is no reason for them to acquire the tramway from Quebec to 'St. Joachim, which pays its way. But I would say to the Government, as being interested in the welfare of the north shore of the river St. Lawrence, that the Government should help towards the completion of the road from St. Joachim to Nairn Falls. Really I cannot object to that, because there is a large and old settled population in that district, and that population really requires some mode of transportation. In that respect I may say that I have received a letter from the President of the Board of Trade of Quebec, a well known gentleman, Mr. J. G. Scott. I shall read his letter:
Quebec, 9th May, 1916.
Dear Mr. Lemieux,-May I take the liberty of writing you a line with regard to the Quebec and Saguenay railway.
I think the people of Quebec are pretty nearly unanimous in approving the course of the Government in making this railway part of the Transcontinental. I know that in the Board of Trade-of which I am the president, and we have a very influential board of nearly 600 members-there has never been a dissenting voice, when the matter has been discussed as it often has. Our people feel that the people of Montmorency, Charlevoix and Saguenay, a large population, have as good claims as those of the Northwest to railway facilities and that this project will help towards winter navigation, or at least the prolongation of the season, a matter which is very dear to us in Quebec.
Moreover, a great many people in Quebec are interested financially, and the failure of this project would not only cause them to lose their money, but it would injure the city generally and perhaps cause us to pay dearer for gas and electricity-We pay too dear as it is.
Yours truly,
J. G. Scott.
I have not the copy of my answer, but I wrote back to Mr. Scott that I was certainly not opposed to the Government helping towards the completion of the road between St. Joachim and Murray Bay, provided the people who had invested their good, sound money in that enterprise were recouped. I may be treading on dangerous ground, but I wish to say that this part of the Quebec and Saguenay, which runs from St. Joachim, the terminus of a good paying tram line, to Nairn Falls, was financed in France.
I do not think that any Canadian money was invested in that section. If I am wrong my hon. friend from Charlevoix (Sir Rodolphe Forget) will correct me.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: About $1,250,000 of Canadian money was invested and $4,600,000 from France.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I have the various prospectuses which were issued in France at the time when this enterprise took form, and the people in France were induced to-invest their money not only in that enterprise, but in a series of enterprises, which were known as the Quebec merger, and which included the Quebec and Saguenay railway, the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix railway, the Quebec Public Utilities, that is, Gas, Electricity, and so on, and the Lotbiniere and Megantic railway. As my hon. friend from Charlevoix said, they parted with their money on the strength of the statements made in these prospectuses. We know how people abroad are induced to invest their money. The French people thought that this would be quite a remunerative enterprise, and they paid their good money in the hope that they would get good returns.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Is my ihon. friend aware that these good French people got back their good money plus 6 and 8 per cent of interest?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: The whole enterprise was guaranteed by the Quebec merger, and the bondholders of the company received their interest, if I am well informed.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
And the
money for their bonds.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: That is the point. I am informed-my hon. friend knows better than I do-that the French bondholders were offered 40 and 50 cents on the dollar for their bonds, and that afraid, as they were, at the failure of the company to proceed with the work, and discouraged, as they were, by the reports of their engineer, they parted with their bonds. It seems to me that in all fairness, and in all justice, these French bondholders, who very cheerfully and very willingly invested their money in that enterprise, should be reimbursed up to the figure which they paid when they subscribed for the bonds of the concern.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Have they not sold their bonds outright, and lost possession of them ?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Yes, that is what I am stating. The French public admittedly-my hon. friend from Charlevoix says so, and he knows better than anybody else-subscribed to the amount of over $4,600,000. They paid that amount in hard cash. The money was spent on the roadbed, on the grading on the small section of the railroad which runs from Murray Bay to Nairn Falls. Nobody will deny that since then French investors have seen their folly. They have been acquainted with the fact that the enterprise was a failure and I say that without any disparagement. It was a serious failure; they were induced to sell their bonds to a committee of purchasers.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: By whom were they induced to sell?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I have the information here.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Would my
hon. friend say that the French people who invested in Canadian Pacific railway stock at 280 and sold it at 165 should be reimbursed?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I am not speaking of
the Canadian Pacific railway. I believe that the bondholders of the Canadian Pacific railway in France and England, and all the world over, are quite satisfied with their stock even at the low figure to which it has fallen, because it is a gilt-edged security. There is no comparison.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Yes, there is.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: In the present instance the French people were induced by rosy prospectuses to invest their good money in this enterprise when the name of Canada was very prominent and very popular in the French money market. I have all the various prospectuses here, but I will not read them. Those people invested their money, and now the Government of Canada proposes to acquire these lines of railway. The Government declares that it will buy the bonds at their par value for the section running from Quebec to St. Joachim. Why not pay the French people the par value on their bonds for the. section from St. Joachim to Nairn's Falls. That would be dealing out equal justice. It seems to me that the French people should be treated by this Government in a fair way. Why one policy for one section of railway, and another policy in regard to the other section? My hon. friend from Charlevoix asked a moment ago who offered to purchase the bonds.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Who induced them to sell?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I have here a copy of
L'Office National des Valeurs Mobilieres, a financial review published in Paris. I will translate the paragraph into English. It reads as follows:
The Defence Committee-
They appointed a Defence Committee in Paris.
The Defence Committee of the bondholders of the Quebec railway, Saguenay and Eastern, have been offered the total purchase of their bonds in Prance at the cost of $60, plus payment of all the coupons due.-
[DOT]-the committee has consented to present that for the bondholders, but as requested, before their doing that, indisputable guarantees are to be given which guarantees have not yet been given by the group.
I do not know what that group is but I answer that my hon. friend induced the French bondholders to accept $60 for their bonds. I do not say that originally they paid $100 for their bonds.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: They paid $82 and some $84.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Well, certainly, offers
were made by a Canadian group through the Committee of Defence of Bondholders in Paris, at $60 for each bond for which they paid, as the minister says, $82.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I wish I could get the same amount for some bonds I have now.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I would like to know where the protection will be for the people

who have built that section of road. How will they be reimbursed? I am not opposed to the Government aiding that section of road but I am opposed to the acquisition of the Lotbiniere and Megantic. I say that this last proposition is absolutely indefensible because this road occupies a territory served by the Intercolonial railway for many years past and nobody in that district has made a demand that the Government should acquire that road. As regards the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix, I do not see why the Government acquires that tramway. It is a good tramway and it pays well.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: It is not a tramway; it is a railway with a federal charter, run by steam and electricity, and it has a telegraph office in many stations. There is a tramway to serve local traffic.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Is it double-tracked?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Doubletracked and both tracks 'are electrified.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: My hon. friend says that this road is not in need of help. It serves a large population, and the people are not anxious that their railway should be absorbed by the Transcontinental. The people I am caring for particularly are the people on the line from St. Joachim to Murray Bay. Let the Government help to complete the line. I would not object to that, but I say that if they are still determined to acquire that line the least they can do is to recoup those who have built it. The hon. member for Charlevoix himself admits that the French investors have sunk in that railway $4,600,000.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: They got back their money and they got 6 to 8 per cent interest on it.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Did they get their capital back? Surely my hon. friend does not contend that the French investors have had returned all their capital invested?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The road
must be given free of encumbrance; that is, the lien on that road must be released.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: By whom?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: By the Quebec Railway Company.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: That comes to exactly what I said a moment ago. The French investors were induced to put their money into the construction of that road, the Canadian company accepted their money, they located the road, they surveyed it, they graded it; to-day the Government will acquire that road free of encumbrance. I am told and my hon. friend says that the Quebec Railway Company will wipe out any encumtoranc existing on it. It means, therefore, that the Quebec Railway Company has purchased the bonds from the French investors.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
make the matter clearer I will thank him for it. All 1 have in mind is to protect the rights of those who have invested their money.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman,-

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: My hon. friend will pardon me; I would like my hon. friend from Charlevoix to give me an explanation. Who has disinterested the French bondholders and how much was paid to them?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: They disinterested themselves by getting rid of their bonds.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Who purchased the
bonds?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I do not know; they were sold on the Paris Bourse, and I do not know who bought them. A great part of them were exchanged for Canadian bonds at 50. The Canadian bonds are now selling at 70, which gives them a premium of ten francs on their money, plus 6 to 8 per cent interest. That came about because friends of mine in Paris asked, as the value of the rentes stood at the ratio of 94 to 60, if we could give 60 for these Canadian bonds, as it would help to bring the French rate of exchange up to 60. I said that I would do so. We got some of our friends together, and we m-ade that offer, but it has never been taken advantage of.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Even on the statement made by the hon. member for Charlevoix, there is the admission that the French investors, although they invested their money in good faith for the building of a Canadian enterprise, will be deprived of a part of the value of the bonds which they secured. I am not opposed to the completion of that section of the railway. I am in favour of it, but I do not say that the Government should acquire the road. The Government has not the means to acquire any railway,

especially when the Government comes before Parliament with the declaration that before long this country may be obliged to nationalize the three transcontinental railways. But I say:	let the Government
help substantially the Quebec and Saguenay portion of the line and they will get my unreserved support. If the Government acquire that railway, which is not built, but which is graded, and in which the French people have sunk so many millions of dollars, the least the Government can do is to protect those unfortunate bondholders. My hon. friend from Mont-magny (Mr. L'Esperanee) smiles. Unless I am a simpleton, I do not see how else the Government can conscientiously act. Is it fair-I put it to my hon. friend, as a friend of the Quebec district-that the people in France who have invested their money after having read the alluring prospectuses which were distributed throughout France should be eliminated and that they should only save a part of their investment5 Is it fair for the Government to take over the road and return to the French investors only a portion of the money they invested? My hon. friend from Charlevoix has admitted that the bonds of the road were undersold to a Canadian group of financiers.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Were exchanged.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: If my hon. friend would only be as frank as he usually is and unravel the whole thing, he would tell us that a group of financiers in Montreal and Quebec, knowing that the bonds would largely increase in value later on, induced the French investors to sell their bonds at a low figure.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: The company has never induced anybody to sell their bonds. The bonds are quoted on the Paris Bourse, and I know that some have been sold on that exchange. This is no more unfair than when I was induced to buy 500,000 francs of the Est Parisien Tramway Company and only got back 5,000 francs. My hon. friend might as well say that the Grand Trunk shareholders and bondholders who invested their money in this country thirty or forty years ago ought to be reimbursed.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend may think what he likes about that, but I am loath to believe that the French would induce foreigners to invest their money in an enterprise under false pretenses.
[Mr. Lemieux.3

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: You know the Est Parisien Company.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I do not know about that. I know that they are very severe in France on schemers.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: 'Your friend ex-Controller Macdonald of Montreal was manager of it.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: He is more your friend than mine. I understand that ex-Controller Macdonald was employed by my hon. friend when he was 'Connected with the Montreal Tramways. I think the Government should see that the French are reimbursed for the money they have invested in this enterprise. I should like to ask the Acting Minister of Railways whether interested parties will be able to bring their claims before the Exchequer Court when this matter comes up?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: The Exchequer Court will determine the value of the properties, also any claims, I suppose, against the road. The owners must give us a clear title.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
must acknowledge that whatever money is paid for the Quebec and Saguenay railway must go to those who have first claim on it; that is, the bondholders. Therefore, the bondholders will 'be paid in full up to the purchase price of the road, and the only way to pay them further, if the purchase price is not sufficient, would be to-add to that purchase price, and we do not feel we can do that.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I do not think any one will object to the building of a road that is a reasonable proposition, and that the country is well able to afford. In the last few days it has frequently been impressed upon the House by hon. gentlemen on both sides that we have overbuilt in this country, and that the time had come when we should cease to extend our railway mileage. The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) pointed out yesterday that there are in this country 2,500 miles of track that should be taken up and laid elsewhere. The Minister of Finance also touched upon this subject yesterday, and his whole argument was that the railway companies should go to the provinces for assistance in completing their lines. The Minister of Finance is not here to-day, and I do not wonder at it.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: He was here a moment ago.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: He is ashamed to be present and countenance this proceeding.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: That is absurd. He was here only a moment ago.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: The Minister of Finance said yesterday that if the company wanted assistance for its incomplete line in Alberta it ought to go to the Government of Alberta, and similarly with Saskatchewan, and the Solicitor General took the same ground. He said that if the provinces wanted the roads completed they should assist them, because we were not in a financial position to do it. One point that has not been touched on, I think, is the assistance these roads have received from the province of Quebec.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I mentioned that last night. The road was granted a subsidy of $3,000 a mile, but nothing was ever paid on it.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Was there not a land grant?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Yes, but nothing was ever given on it.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Why?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I do not know why.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member for Charlevoix can tell us.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: This was granted in March, 1912, and the road stopped in August, 1912; so nothing was earned.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: On account of the railroad falling down in its construction they have not received anything from the province of Quebec. But they have received a subsidy from the Dominion Government.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: They have received $132,000.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: On a railway that is incomplete; that is the great objection. Why should the Government at this time, and with financial conditions as they are, take over a tramway running out of the city of Quebec? The hon. member for Charlevoix and the Acting Minister of Railways tell us that the proposition is paying its way. But why take over this particular tramway, even though it has a railway track on which cars can be run? Why should we have anything to do with the Lotbiniere and Megantic, which road, as I understand, is running? The only part that we ought to deal with is that which is uncompleted, the part from St. Joachim to Nairn Falls, a distance of 62 miles. I understand from the statement of the hon. member for Charlevoix that people in France put in $4,600,000.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: That is the par value of the bonds. They were sold at 82.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman is proposing to pay the face value of the bonds.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
In addition to the
$4,600,000 put in by the people of France; $1,500,000, the hon. gentleman says, was put in by the people in Quebec province.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: In Montreal.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Well, in the province of Quebec. That money was put in for this sixty-two miles of railway of which only 87 per cent of the grading is done, and a lot of that washed out. That amounts to $98,000 a mile for grading 87 per cent of a railroad. Either the money was practically taken out of it, or else the country is so rough that it should not have a railway. If the grading of 87 per cent of this mileage costs $98,000 a mile, it will cost $125,000 a mile to put the road in running shape. Now, $125,000 a mile may be a paying proposition in such country as the state of Pennsylvania, where they have trains running every five minutes of the twenty-four hours, but in a sparsely settled country a railway cannot get the traffic that would justify the Government in paying so much money for it.
Why not get down to the facts of the matter? This whole proposition, in my judgment, is nothing but a political steal. And the thirty thousand people along this line are not going to get the advantage. Hon. gentlemen opposite are going to get the advantage, <or the Government i? simpiy paying for the political support they got the other day-that is what it amounts to. At a time when the Minister of Finance says that we are not in a position to go on and build railroads we are called upon to put in ten millions of dollars, and all we get is sixty-two miles of railroad. We are actually told that we are to pay $98,000 a mile for a road on which not a bridge is built, on which not only the rails are not laid, but the grading is not completed, on which there is not a station house, for which there is no telegraph line-absolutely nothing but 87 per cent of the work of grading done. The Minister of Railways has the nerve to come to this House and ask us to put ten millions into such a scheme as that. Of all the propositions that have ever been



put before this House in connection with railroad building-and I know there have been many bad ones in the past, and I am not going to say that one .side is worse than the other-there was never such an outrageous proposition as this. Yesterday we voted $8,000,000 for the Grand Trunk Pacific and $15,000,000 for the Canadian Northern. Are you awaTe, Mr. Chairman, I opposed these grants? But there is this to be said in connection with the Canadian Northern-that the provinces of Canada and the Dominion of Canada combined have already put in $208,000,000 into that system. So, we were committed to a certain extent. But here is a gigantic piece of folly, simply a political proposition, by which the Government wants to recoup some of its political friends and supporters, and to that end asks Parliament to vote $10,000,000 to add 62 miles to the railways of Canada. I have never heard anything like it; and if this Government persists in such a proposition, especially in these times, it should be driven, from power.
See what this proposal means. The Minister of Finance is putting a business impost on the people of Canada by which he proposes to tax every business man coming within the scope of his Bill 25 per cent on what he earns in bis business over 7 per cent. By this tax he expects to raise about $25,000,000 a year. And now it is proposed that a sum equal to more than one-third of this special tax for a year is to be paid for a railway 62 miles long serving a country with only 30,000 people. ,
Let us put it in another way. From the Atlantic to the Pacific the people of Canada, men, women and children, have been busy since this war began paying, working, doing everything that was in their power to maintain the Patriotic Fund, the Red Cross Fund and others intended to. alleviate the sufferings of our men at the front. And the whole of that amount so contributed in a year, if I remember the figures correctly, would not amount to what this Government here proposes to hand over to a few men. Montreal put up a million or two, Toronto a million or two; the provinces put up large sums of money, and all this money is taken with one hand and thrown into this concern with the other. With this money it is proposed to take over railroads that, at the price suggested, will be a millstone around the neck of the Dominion of Canada^as long as the Dominion of Canada lasts. I am not opposed to helping railroads in the province of Quebec. Quebec is my native 
province. There I was bom and brought up and I have always had the kindliest feelings for my old province of Quebec. If this road is in the condition that it is represented to be in, let the Government come forward with a sane, reasonable proposal to put that 62 miles of road on its feet and add it to the mileage of the railways of Canada. No man would support that quicker than I would, because that would be a reasonable proposition. This company got hold of French bonds at 60 cents on the dollar, for which they are now going to get 100 cents on the dollar from my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Railways. Then, we are going to issue $4,400.000 of securities that can be turned into cash; these we are going to hand over to the present stockholders, a little group of men who have manipulated the French bondholders and every one else. In this political deal they are now going to draw $4,400,000 out of the Treasury for their own purposes. And that is not the end of the trouble. In addition to that, the Acting Minister of Railways has to complete those roads. He has to add to the roads that are now operating and also to complete this 62 miles of road.
I have pointed out on more than one occasion that within five years we shall have a debt of about $2,000,000,000, with an annual interest charge of $100,000,000. My hon. friend the Acting Minister of Railways now deliberately proposes to add another half million to our yearly interest account. I say again that if this Parliament passes this measure they will have to take the responsibility before the people of Canada, and I venture to say that the people of Canada will not justify that action in any shape or form. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) suggested a much better way to spend this money and at the same time get value for it-by building up transcontinental railway facilities in the city of Quebec. If you do that, and this railway is as advantageous as hon. gentlemen opposite say it is, the province of Quebec will come to the rescue of this railway company and see it through. But the Government and the Legislature of the province of Quebec, who know the circumstances much better than we do, would not justify what has been done in connection with this road, would not justify the expenditure of $98,000 a mile on an uncompleted grade. The thing is too absurd for argument. That is one reason why this

Bill should be defeated-so that members of the House and the people of the country should have an opportunity of getting some information on the' subject. We have not been able to get any information worth speaking about from my hon. friend the acting minister or from the Solicitor General. The very fact that the Acting Minister of Railways has to get the Solicitor General at his elbow to wiggle and twist and turn this thing around is 5 p.m. enough to .make the people suspicious as to the merits of the case. The Solicitor General i6 very adroit on railway matters and when we see the Solicitor General take his place at the acting minister's elbow, we know that the acting minister is in deep water. Not knowing what to do, he send3 out an S.O.S. call and the Solicitor General rushes to his rescue. Well, the Solicitor General may be able to engineer this legislation through, but he will have to take a good deal of responsibility for it.
The hon. member for Charlevoix spoke about a winter port. I am free to admit that the hon. member ought to know more about that than I do, for it is now over forty years since I left the province of Quebec. But I have seen twenty vessels frozen in the ice in the month of November.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: On the south shore?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: On the south shore. If my hon. friend is right in saying that Murray Bay can be made an open port-I think it is'only 40 miles from Quebec, is it not?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: 90 miles.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
From St.
Catherine's bay, 130 miles.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Of course, the further
you get down the easier it is to navigate in winter. Ice-breaking steamers have had a great deal of difficulty at times in navigating the St. Lawrence during the winter months. I do not know of any vessels other than ice-breakers that have navigated to any considerable extent during the winter months, and you cannot have all your freight steamers built as ice-breakers. In my judgment it will be many years before you will have a winter port any place along the St. Lawrence where it is as narrow as it is at St. Catherine's bay. I will not be too sure about that, however, because I am not as well posted as my hon. friend is.
If the Government does intend to carry out this proposed legislation why do they
254i
not do it in a businesslike way? What is the reason why the Railway Department should not deal with this matter? I will tell you the reason: it is right there among the papers that have been brought down. Their own engineer gives the value of thd property a trifle over half what my hon. friend the Solicitor General and the Acting Minister of Railways are prepared to pay. This is not a matter that ought to go before the Exchequer Court. The Exchequer Court, as I understand the matter, was established in order that any one 'having a claim against the Government might go there to have that claim settled. Who has a claim against the Government in connection with these three railways? We gave them a subsidy; we do not owe them a dollar. The Intercolonial doe's not need the roads, nor does the Grand Trunk Pacific need them. We have no liability; we have no responsibility, therefore why go to the Exchequer Court? This Government is losing all the power of government that it ever had-and it never had much. Commissions are appointed for everything, and now, when they want to take over about 70 miles of operating road and 62 miles of grading, they cannot trust their own engineers and they cannot trust themselves. They cannot trust themselves, and so they pass a Bill here in order to have an excuse for handing the matter over to the Exchequer Court to have that court pass on the value of the road. They do not even trust the Judge of the Exchequer Court, because they tie his hands behind his back. If this Government are going, to take over this road, why do they not say to the Judge of the Exchequer Court, if they are bound to put it up to him: " Here, go out and value the road, find out whiat it is worth "? My hon. friend the Acting Minister of Railways and the Solicitor General say: No, we must find out how much it cost. When you find that $98,000 per mile was put into 87 per cent of the length of line graded, I do not wonder at the hon. member for Charlevoix (Sir Rodolphe Forget) not wanting the road to be paid for iat its value. I can quite understand how he would prefer to have paid back what the road has cost, or what they claim it has cost. Supposing that, in the locating of that road, as in the case of the locating of a great part of the Canadian Pacific railway when it was first constructed, the worst possible iroute was chosen, -although there were much better routes near at hand, why should this Gov-

eminent, in taking over the road, pay for the mistakes made by those who built the road? Or why should they take it over at more than whiat it is worth to them? We are buying this for the people of Canada.
I ask, is there one man who is sitting on the Government benches to-day who, if he was putting his own money into this road, would take it over on such a plan as this? Would he say: "Well, I will pay you what you put into it with interest on your money "? Or would he say: " I will take the road over at what it is worth to me"? There is the whole position. My hon. friend is putting it to the Judge of the Exchequer Court instead of trusting his own officers. One of his officers has made a Teport showing the value of the road to be about one-half what the Acting Minister of Railways proposes to pay. But the minister refuses to go by that, because it would not enable him to put in a large sum of money to those supporters who sit behind him, and put it in, not to the advantage of the people of the country, but for political advantage and nothing else. I hope that when this matter comes to be fully considered by the Government we will have this Bill withdrawn, and I would ask my hon. friends on the Government benches to consider well what the effect of this will be. If this road is bought under such circumstances, how are the Government going ito get out of taking over the branch lines of the Intercolonial, many of which they have promised to take over? Will the owners of those roads not also demand that they be taken over, not under the Bill that was passed not long ago for the purpose of enabling the Government to take over branch lines, but on the same terms as this road. Do you not see where it leads us? It will be just one thing such as this after another, and that at a time when the Government of the country cannot afford it. We have heard the ministers talking of economy. What economy are they practising? They are bringing forward now, in the dying days of the session, when members cannot post themselves fully on the enormity of what is proposed, legislation of a most important character. I venture to say that we do not know one-half about this matter yet, and they are coming forward 'with a proposal to add another $10,000,000 to the debt of Canada for an enterprise that, I venture to say, will never pay one cent of interest. It will be just like the Intercolonial; if it pays working expenses it will be doing mighty well. So

we shall hlave added $10,000,000 to our debt, which will involve half a million dollars each year for interest as long as time lasts, unless we pay off the principal.
As I said before, this is the most vicious proposition that has ever come before Parliament, and I ask the Acting Minister to take it into his further consideration and decide if, in the interest of the people of Canada, he should not withdraw the Bill; because I know perfectly well that my hon. friend the acting minister cannot go into his own constituency and, before any audience, justify the handing over of this $10,000,000. He cannot go into any .constituency in Canada, except perhaps those that will immediately benefit, and justify this course. I say again I am quite willing that the Government should give the necessary aid to secure the completion of this road; but they should not buy it.
I trust that if anything is done it will be done along the line of assisting the road, not of purchasing it.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The hon. member who has just spoken has made complaint that we have not provided the House with sufficient facts. Of all hon. members of this House, the last who should complain of the absence of provision of facts is the hon. member for Assiniboia. I have never been able to discover that facts are of the slightest value to him; in fact, they seem to impede the progress of his rhetoric rather than to help him. His first task, whenever he gets on his feet, is to divorce himself from anything in the nature of facts and truth, and to. substitute the figments of his fancy, and to proceed with a very well-stocked supply of superlatives to denounce the Government from every standpoint. If I could add to his armoury of adjectives, of superlatives in particular, I know that I would be doing him a great deal more service than if I attempted to supply him with facts on any subject at all.
We have got to that stage of the argument where hon. gentlemen opposite recognize the necessity, from the point of view of the interest of the country itself, of in some way, taking care of the situation with respect to the Quebec and Saguenay railway.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: The uncompleted portion.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The uncompleted portion of it, the Quebec and Saguenay is all uncompleted. For the moment I leave out the other two roads, the Lotbiniere and Me-

gantic and the Montmorency and Charlevoix, which are admitted to be paying concerns by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), who, of all hon. gentlemen opposite, should know beet. The duty of the Government, according to hon. members opposite, is to take care of the situation in respect of the Quebec and Saguenay by reason of the necessity of providing railway service for the inhabitants of that country, numbering not a few thousand but very many, .something in the neighbourhood of 100,000, depending on how far back from the line you go.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
And from the further
point of view of saving to the country the tremendous amount of money already invested in that line and avoiding the necessity of repeating that expenditure when the road comes to be coippleted.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
suggest that that is the position taken on this side of the House?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Yes.	.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I would like to dissociate myself from that position.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The hon. member is
ready to lead his friends all to their fate. He prefers, instead of serving the people along the banks of the St. Lawrence, to build more elevators where those already built are unfilled, and to put a Pullman caT service between Quebec and Cochrane. I understand he wants the Government to operate a Pullman service there, although the prospects are that such a service would get about one passenger a month. That is the alternative proposition put forward by him.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: You could get more traffic between Edmonton and Cochrane' than between Quebec and Nairn Falls.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I question that myself. I would rather undertake to operate six miles than to operate several hundred.
Of course, we all know the railway policy of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). He was a member of the late Government. We know the railway policy of the late Government. He, of all men, has the right, of course, to talk about a blockade in western Canada. The hon. member for Edmonton should know what a blockade in western Canada is, because every year during which he was a member
of that Administration we had a blockade of western wheat.
Every year, during which he was a member of that Administration, the wheat was sent back to the farmers' doors, and they could not get it out for months, yes, sometimes for a year. It was a regular occurrence right up to 1911 and including 1911, and in those days they did not have half the crop that we had last year. The Government, of which my hon. friend was a member, spent millions of dollars on lines that could not be of service for many years to come. What was the railway policy of my hon. friend from Edmonton and of the 'Government of which he was a member? It was a policy of waste and want. Not a dollar to assist 100,000 people on the banks of the St. Lawrence, but millions for the wilds of the north where no human being could live. A policy of freight without railways in one half of the Dominion, and railways without freight in the other. Wheat rotting in Alberta, rails rusting in Quebec. An annual paralysis in western grain; an annual orgy of eastern contractors. That was the railway policy to which the hon. member for Edmonton for seven years adhered. I do not wonder that we dismiss rather hurriedly any suggestions which he offers at the present time.
However, I will take up the more reasonable proposal which seems to be adhered to very generally by hon. gentlemen on the other side, that, in respect to this Quebec and Saguenay railway, instead of taking the railway by virtue of expropriation at a price not to exceed $4,135,000, or not to exceed the actual cost, we should loan sufficient money to enable the owners to complete the road. Let me take that alternative proposition of hon. gentlemen opposite- and they all seem to agree on this, even the hon. member for Edmonton.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: the completion of the Quebec and Saguenay railway, which runs from St. Jean des Ohaillons to Naim Falls.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: That is exactly the alternative I was referring to. Hon. gentlemen opposite want an estimate by way of loan to the Quebec and Saguenay railway for the completion of that line. It would have to be by way of loan, unless we took over -the line. Now hon. gentlemen opposite say that this Bill means an investment of $10,000,000 before the road is complete. It means, first of all, an investment -ithe way we are taking it-of $4,135,000 to get down to details, for the Quebec and Saguenay line, and from that sum comes off $116,000, which is in the trust account, making virtually $4,019,000. There is $330,000 for the Lotbiniere and Megantio line, making a total of $4,349,000, to which add $2,500,000 for the Quebec and Charlevoix line, or a total of $6,849,000. That is the total for the three roads at the outside under the-present Bill, and it will be less unless it is shown that actually that money or more than that -money has gone into the road. Let us suppose that it will reach the maximum of $6,849,000. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that, before this road is completed, the total will have reached $10,000,000. There [DOT] is only one road to complete, the Quebec and Saguenay road, consequently they claim that it will take $3,251,000 to complete the Quebec and Saguenay line, and they >ask this House to put in the Estimates a sum of $3,251,000 by way of loan to the Quebec and Saguenay railway.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I did not.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman did not suggest any method, but he wanted aid to be given to complete the Quebec and Saguenay railway, and he said it would take $10,000,000 altogether, or, in other words, that it would require $3,251,000 to complete that line.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Why n-ot the usual subsidy!'

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: How are you going to complete it with the usuial subsidy, if, as hon. gentlemen opposite say, it will take $3,251,000 to complete it?

speechtext: Let the owners do something.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
said that he would supply a liberal allowance to complete the road, and you cannot

-complete it unless you supply the money, and that, according to hon. gentlemen opposite, is the amount of money that it will take. There is no other way of getting it. The proposition of hon. gentlemen opposite is to loan them $3,251,000.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: It is not.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Then, where would we
be? We would have $6,100,000 in bonds against the road according to the figures given; $4,600,000 of French bonds, and $1,500,000 Canadian, making a total of $6,100,000. We would have a total charge against the road, therefore, of $9,351,000, and we would have a second mortgage.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I wish to state absolutely and positively that I for one did not say, and I did not hear any one else on this side say, that we ought to put in the Estimates three million, and some odd thousand dollars to complete the road. The hon. member is putting words in our mouths that we never uttered, and he knows it.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: That is the only contention the hon. member could make unless he was talking absolute nonsense. What is the use of talking about voting $3,000 a mile when he says it will take $10,000.0 to complete the road. Our maximum is $6,849,000, and, according to the contention of my hon. friends, that leaves $3,251,000 as the balance necessary to complete it. You cannot complete it in any other way.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend lay down the proposition that the owners should not do anything?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I am laying down no
proposition; it is the hon. member's proposition that I am dealing with. I say that there is no way of completing the road except by providing the money, and when they come before Parliament and talk about voting $3,000 a mile, hon. gentlemen opposite are talking nonsense, and transparent nonsense.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Might I suggest-

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
will have time to make any suggestions he pleases, and I will commend him for doing so.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
What the hon. member for Assiniboia said was, as I understood him, that he was willing to aid the road. He did not say that he was willing to build it. I take it that he meant he was willing to

give the ordinary railway subsidy, and it would then be for the owners to find the money and to finish the road. It is their road, not ours.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: The ordinary subsidy has been given, and it has failed to complete the road. Nothing else w'ill complete it except the provision of money; the company are at the end of their tether. The position of hon. gentlemen opposite was as I have stated, until they saw that they were caught.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I beg the hon. member's pardon, he must not assert a position that does not exist.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member for Edmonton did so; I did not charge him, but the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) and the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) advocated that we should provide the money to complete the road.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I state absolutely that I did not, and that the Solicitor General is deliberately putting words in my mouth that are absolutely false.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Order. I must ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw that statement.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I will withdraw that statement when the Solicitor General withdraws his, and not before.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I do not think that the conduct of debates in this House will be assisted by the hon. member taking up that attitude, and I think the hon. member will be the first to realize it. If there is any. point of order to be raised in regard _ to anything that the Solicitor General said,
' I will be very happy to deal with it. As I understood him, the Solicitor General was making an argument on a general statement which he assumed had been made by hon. gentlemen opposite. I did not understand his remarks in any other way. I must ask the hon. member for Assiniboia to withdraw his remark, as it is clearly out of order.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
In deference to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, and as I do not wish to trespass on the rules of the House, I will withdraw the statement, and I will now ask that the Solicitor General withdraw the statement which he made and which I absolutely deny. I say that there was not one word of truth in the statement
which the Solicitor General made. I ask him to withdraw the statement.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: If I have in any way mis-stated what the hon. gentleman said, all I have to say is that the way I put it was much more sensible than the way he put it, and the way that does far more credit to his intelligence.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I want that statement
withdrawn.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I do not apprehend that the Solicitor General refused to accept the statement of the hon. member for Assiniboia. Will the hon. member for Assiniboia state what particular remark of the Solicitor General he objects to.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: The Solicitor General stated, referring to. me, that the members on this side of the House proposed to advance to this uncompleted road from St. Joachim to Nairn Falls over $3,000,000. I never made any such statement, and I would like the Solicitor General to acknowledge that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: As I understand, the Solicitor General never said that the hon. member for Assiniboia did say so. I understood him to say that that was the logical effect of the argument made by the hon. gentleman, and if that is so, I do not see how any complaint can be made.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Well, I will let it go at that. We have one sort of ruling for one side of the House and another for the other.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: What the Chairman says I was arguing is exactly what I was arguing, and, unless the hon. gentleman's statement means that, I am afraid it does discredit to his intelligence. In the interval, I have been doing a little figuring to ascertain what the hon. gentleman's contention would really mean. He states to the House-and these are hi's figures, not mine-that it will take $10,000,000 altogether to these roads complete, and $3,251,000 to complete the Quebec and Saguenay. The $10,000,000 is his own figure. That, I find amounts to about $55,000 a mile. He proposes to get a $55,000-a-mile road completed by a grant -of $1,200 a mile. That is the suggestion of the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
knows better than that.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: I know that I know better, but the hon. gentleman does not.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: My hon. friend knows as well as any member of this House that the subsidy give'' a railway that costs ias much a9 has already been expended on this is $6,400 a mile.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I will help the hon.
gentleman out to that extent. That would be $6,400 a mile, which would leave about $49,000 a mile to be provided, and he wants to suggest to this House that we would be taking care of the situation and be providing to complete the road by supplying $6,400 a mile out of $55,000.
Mr. TURRIFF; I never said anything of the kind.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext: Does not the hon. gentleman see the almost childish nonsense of such a suggestion?

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
No, I do not; my hon.
friend is still mis-stating everything I said.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's
own way of putting it means that we would supply $6,400 more per mile in the vain and delusive hope that we would acquire from some one else the $49,000 or $50,000 a mile still necessary to complete the road.
Mr. OLIVER; This is not our road.
Mr, MEIGHEN; I know it is not, but hon. members behind my hon. friend say that it is our duty to see it completed. We could only get it completed by giving the company a loan of money. Every other means have been exhausted. There are against the Toad to-day some $6,100,000 in , bonds; at all events there is about $5,000,000 against it in bonds, and the rest is against it in some .form or other. But, take it at $5,000,000: it means that we would be taking a second mortgage for whatever sum we advanced subject to a mortgage of $5,000,000. Now, we are getting the whole road in its present condition for a trifle oveT $4,000,000 from the owners. I appeal to my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) to say if that is not better business, if it is not better policy, than to advance against the road with a $5,000,000 mortgage ahead of us the sum of $3,251,000. Is that policy not preferable to the one advocated by the hon. member for Rouville?
I believe the hon. member for Rouville wants to be fair. I do. not think that he saw when he was arguing that it would take the money that he said it would. What would become of it according to hie own argument? As a matter of fact it would not take that money because we do

not propose to invest $10,000,000. These are the figures of hon. gentlemen opposite. But, it would never pay this country, and it would never be business, to make a loan on this Quebec and Saguenay railway and have that loan subject to the mortgage indebtedness that is now against it when we have the other alternative of getting the line for $4,019,000. I appeal to the business- sense of the members of this House if it is not better to take over this Toad at a cost to this country of $4,019,000 than to advance money into the hands of these people-the Quebec and Saguenay Railway Company-and take a lien against it subject to a charge of $5,000,000.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOTBINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
As we are now in the dying days of the session, I think it might be well that we should try to come to a perfectly solid basis for discussion of this very important question, because a great many of the arguments which have been presented are irrelevant and unfounded in fact. The hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) has stated that these three railways which are to be acquired by the Government, and which are to be made part of the Government Railway system, will assist 100,000 people. He is altogether in error as to that. Take first the Lot-binifere and Megantic railway. That railway extends from the St. Lawrence up to the Grand Trunk in the county of Megan-tic. Some hon. gentleman stated, I think the hon. member for Charlevoix (Sir Ro-dolphe Forget), that the county of Megantic would be assisted by this road. The county of Megantic has a population of about 20,000 souk, but this road is of no use at all to that county. The people of Lyster, which is at the extremity of the county, going to Montreal and Quebec, are better served by the Grand Trunk than they will be by this railway. This railway would be useful to part of the population of Lot-biniere, a small number; but, as far as that goes, I do not object that it should be made part of the Government system. Now, we come to the other side of the river. The two railways on the north shore, the Quebec, Montmorency and Charlevoix and the Quebec and Saguenay, will serve part of the population of the county of Quebec, perhaps 20,000, and of the county of Charlevoix, perhaps 20,000. The line will be of no assistance whatever to the people of Chicoutimi and Saguenay unless it is extended from Murray Bay to the Saguenay river. Then, of course, it will be of some

use to the people of that district; hut otherwise I do not think it will serve anybody. An argument which has been presented here, and which has etruck me as having force, is that there are in that part of the country people who are amongst the oldest settlers in the country, and who have no railway communication at all. But the railway will not serve the purpose which I heard mentioned yesterday by the hon. Acting Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid), who said that it would develop agriculture in that part of the country. It cannot be developed more than it is. The country is- mountainous, but it ie pretty well settled now. It might develop the lumbering industry somewhat, but I doubt if the lumbering or any other industry would be better served than it is served at the present time by the river. But people, in these modern days, want to have railway communication, and the people here have been for a long time led to believe they would have railway communication. They have been deceived in that expectation.
It is very unfortunate for the people of that locality that the company has found itself unable to complete the enterprise. I do not know the circumstances very well, but it was not for lack of funds, because according to the statement made by the Acting Minister of Railways yesterday, the company had expended upon that part of the railway between Quebec and Saguenay a little over $5,000,000. The distance from St. Joachim to Murray Bay is about 62 miles, and from Murray Bay to Nairn Palls about 6 miles; say 70 miles altogether. Surely $5,000,000 was ample with which to complete a railway of this character. I know the locality very well, and it is not a difficult country to build through, except in one part when you come to Cap Tourmente. The rest of the road is per fectly level, and where that obtains Tailway construction is always easy. Labour was also at hand and there were no obstacles of any kind. So, in my estimation, the company had ample means with which to complete the road, but they have failed to do so. I do not want to be severe or to pass judgment. I only know that the people of that locality for want of the company extending this railway, are without . communication for the greater part of the year. The usefulness of the railway has been recognized by all Governments. The Dominion Government subsidized it in the ordinary way to the extent of $6,400 a mile, and the Quebec Government also gave subsidies to a large amount; I do not know the precise amount, but I understand it was fairly generous. With all this assistance the company should have been able to construct the road and have it in operation to-day. But it has not done so. However, the people must not suffer; I admit that.
I am prepared to take a generous view of this business and give the assistance to which the people in that part of the country are entitled. It is true we are living in strenuous times, and that perhaps now is not the most propitious time we could choose; it is true also that we should be as careful as possible about launching into new enterprises. Unfortunately, this is not a new enterprise, and for my part I should like to see it completed. .
But I should like to know why the Government are proceeding in this way. Last year they introduced a Bill [DOT] for the acquisition of branch lines. Why do. they not proceed under that Bill to acquire the roads in question? Why are they changing their mode of procedure? The present method is full of difficulties. Let me read what the Bill says:
1.	The Governor in Council may authorize and empower the Minister of Railways and Canals to acquire, under the provisions of an Act to amend the Government Railways Act and to authorize the purchase of certain railways, chapter sixteen of the statutes of 1915, and upon such terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may approve, the railways described in the schedule hereto, together with such equipment, appurtenances and properties used in connection with such railways as the Governor in Council may deem necessary for the operation thereof.
2.	The consideration to be paid for each of the said railways and for any equipment, appurtenances and properties that may be acquired as aforesaid shall be the value thereof as determined by the Exchequer Court of Canada.
The price is to be determined by the Exchequer Court. It may be $1,000,000, $2,000,000 or $4,000,000, whatever the judge decides. So far, so good. Then the money is to be paid to whom? The price so fixed by the Exchequer Court is to be paid by the Governor in Council to parties who are not even mentioned here. Just before six o'clock I understood the leader of the Opposition to intimate that under chapter 16 of the statutes of 1915, under which, with the additional clauses that are inserted, it is proposed to acquire the railways in question, we would be obligated to come to Parliament later for ratification of the agreement that we might enter into with the owners of these railways for the purchase. He asked whether, if that were the case, we would come back to Parliament later with the agreement that we would make in this case. My reply to him was that, while I did riot recollect such a clause being in the Act of 1915, I felt that, as we were proposing to act under the authority of that statute, we would be subject to all its obligations, and that if that were one of those obligations, we would be subject to it. I promised to let the committee know at eight o'clock. I find, however, upon reference to the statute, that, if I understood the right hpn. gentleman aright, there is no such clause. The statute of 1915 provides that we may acquire roads by purchase or by expropriation, gives certain powers to and imposes certain obligations upon the minister and makes certain conditions. Among the conditions is this: No purchase shall be complete until the money is voted by Parliament for the purpose. But there is' no provision to the effect that the agreement so made, embodying such terms and conditions as it may emibody, must afterwards be ratified by any special act or

action of this Parliament. We are in just the same position now. We come to Parliament with this Bill; we propose to acquire by this Bill certain railways, the acquiring to be done under the provisions of the .statute of 1915. We shall be obligated by all the provisions of that statute; but there is no provision that we should come back to Parliament with our agreement, whatever the agreement might be. We do, of course, have to come to Parliament for the appropriation, and we shall have to come to Parliament for the appropriation in this case just as in the other.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOT-BINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
The clause to which I referred is in these words:
Provided further that no contract for the construction of a line of railway exceeding 25 miles in length shall be entered into or the purchase price of any such railway or other work be paid until after a sum of money for the purpose has been appropriated by Parliament.

That applies in this

speechtext: I am not sure that it applies in this case. You depart from the statute. If you had proceeded under the statute the Minister of Railways should have made an agreement with the company for the purchase of that road, and then you would have to come to Parliament. But here, as I understand the Bill, the contract is complete the moment this Bill becomes, law. There are two conditions-the fixing of the price, which is left to the Exchequer Court, and the application of the price so determined. When these two conditions shall have been fulfilled, in my judgment this Paliament will have lost all its control. Of course, the money will not be paid until it has been appropraited by Parliament; but when this Act has been passed, when the court, acting under this legislation, has fixed a price, would it be within, the power of this Parliament not to make the appropriation? This would be a contract binding upon Parliament, and that is why I say that we should provide here that in any case the contract which is to be made, the application of the money, and all the conditions of the purchase should be referred to Parliament.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOT-BINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.

The right hon. gentleman said that under our Bill we have two conditions to be fulfilled, and he apprehends that these will be all we need to fulfill. Well, I do not know that I could limit them to two. Certainly one condition is

very essential: that the price must be ratified by the Exchequer Court.

speechtext: Must be fixed by the Exchequer Court. And necessarily there will be conditions, as to the purchase, because certain matters in respect to power and the possibility of competing lines, etc., have to be taken care of in the interest of the country, and these conditions are especially provided for in this Bill. But, none the less, all the provisions and all the conditions that are in chapter 16 of the statutes of 1915 are binding upon us; there is no doubt about that. The condition as to the precedent of a vote by Parliament is just as binding in respect of this purchase as in respect of any purchase or acquirement under the Act of 1915-just as binding, but not more binding. There is nothing in the statute of 1915 as to when the appropriation shall be made by Parliament; but it must antecede the going into effect of the acquiring contract. The same is true here: the appropriation by Parliament, whatever it may be, must antecede the going into effect of the acquiring contract. We are under all the obligations of the Act of 1915 and the additional obligations of this Act. The obligations of the Act of 1915 apply with exactly the same, and no more, effect to this acquirement as to any other acquirement under that Act.
