maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOT-BINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
Before this Bill passes I want to enter my protest against this measure. I have not hitherto participated in the discussion, chiefly because I was not very well acquainted with the facts. I biave been listening to the discussion last night and this afternoon, and have learned something with regard to the proposal, and I think that I would not be doing my duty to my constituents if I did not place myself on record as opposed to it. The condition of our finances in Canada is becoming alarming. Everyone will admit that we are face to face with a very large expenditure. The appropriations already made in conneo tion with the war, and the enormous expenditures in which we shall have to share, that are now being incurred in Europe for war materials and for other purposes in carrying on the war, will probably, at the end of the present year, amount to at least one billion dollars. The interest on

this enormous sum will exhaust more than one half the current revenue of this country; and, in the face of these enormous expenditures that are confronting us, it appears to me to be most reckless for the Government to embark upon an expenditure of this kind. The credit of the country will be affected by the liabilities that we are incurring during the present session. Our credit is not as good now as it was three or four years ago. The little province of Nova Scotia is able to-day to secure money in the United States at a lower rate of interest than the Dominion of Canada. That was not the case five years dgo, but it is the case to-day, showing you that the way in which we are embarking on these extravagant liabilities i& affecting the credit of this Dominion to a very alarming extent. One would suppose that the liabilities that are being incurred at the present time would have acted as a check upon the Government in regard to incurring further liabilities; but during the present session our proposed capital expenditure amounts, if I remember rightly, to somewhere in the neighbourhood of $50,000,000. That is an enormous amount to add to our liabilities in one year, altogether independently of the war. That strikes me as unjustifiable and as endangering the future credit of the country. In my own constituency, when railroad extension was asked for, the Minister of Railways told me that it was impossible to do anything in that part of Canada at the present time, owing to the fact that the Minister of Finance was unable to provide the funds. He said that if the Finance Minister could provide the funds there would be no question at all about going on with that very necessary expenditure. This was the answer he gave me.
Mr. Sinclair: I understand that the minister says he would build these branch lines this year if the Minister of Finance could furnish the money.
Mr. Reid: I said that while the war was on I would not ask for money for this railway.
I was satisfied with that reason, because the war is on and we are incurring enormous expenditures in connection with it. I intended to explain that to my constituents, and I felt that it was a fair explanation. But what am I to say now? Am I to go back and tell them that since this statement was made to me by the acting Minister of Railways, he has asked this House to vote $15,000,000 for the Canadian Northern railway, $8,000,000 for the Grand Trunk Pacific, and is involving us to-day in a liability which it is estimated will amount in the end to about $10,000,000? The large appropriations to the Canadian Northern railway and to the Grand Trunk Pacific can be justified on national grounds. It may be said that these are great national undertakings and that they must be kept up. I see the force of that argument. But that argument does not apply to the railways that we are proposing to take over under this agreement. I fear that we shall not be able to accept the sincerity of the acting Minister of Railways, who assured me that the only reason why he refused to entertain any further railway extension in the province of Nova Scotia was that there was no money available for that purpose. The minister should explain why he discriminates in this way between one province and another. The statement has been made by the Solicitor General that this railway will accommodate some 30,000 people. The railway that was proposed in eastern Nova Scotia, to which I am referring, would have accommodated more than 30,000 people. It is estimated that it would accommodate about 40,000 people, and it could be built for about one-quarter of the expenditure we are proposing to make in connection with this railway.
The Prime Minister himself gave a promise some few years ago that that railway to which I am referring would be - built. I would expect the Prime Minister, before embarking on a wild -scheme of this kind, to think of the pledges he had given in my constituency. Those pledges ought to be kept. I fear, Sir, that the true reason is not a public reason. The true reason dates 'back to the election of 1911. My hon. friend from -Charlevoix (Sir Rodolphe Forget), as every one knows, was a very prominent supporter of this Government in that election. He came back after September, 1911, to this- House with quite a number of scalps in his belt, and now the people of Canada -are expected to pay this very large price for his services on that occasion. I have heard that several men have been claiming the leadership of the Nationalist party in the province of Quebec. At one time we were told it wa3 Mr. Bourassa; another .time Mr. Armand Lavergne claimed that honour, and the Secretary of State (Mr. Patenaude) has also been named in connection with it. But I think, we may say that the real chief of the Nationalist party in the province of Quebec, the one who has stood behind that party and who has brought its members here, is my hon. friend from Charlevoix. $10,000,000 is a very large

price to pay for about 20 Nationalists who support the Government in this House. That is about half a million dollars apiece that the people of Canada are asked to pay for their services. The Prime Minister himself will admit that half a million dollars is a very large price to pay for a Nationalist.
In the other Chamber a discussion took place a few days ago in regard to the war, and an hon. gentleman there, who has been very prominent in connection with this scheme of the Quebec and Saguenay railway, made a speech in which he condemned the Government for spending so much money in connection -with recruiting and the war.
He said it would be far better to put the money in the Quebec and Saguenay railway than to spend it in assisting the Empire in this war. I thought that that was a very impertinent proposal when I read it in the Hansard of the other chamber, but it never entered my mind that within two or three weeks the Government would accept the advice of that hon. gentleman and do what he told them to do with the public money. If we were building railways, I could make a great many comparisons showing the necessity for railway extension in other parts of Canada; that is, if we were building railways in the public interest. But, as we are paying political debts with this appropriation, and not building railways at all, it would not be worth while to enter into any discussion as to what might be done with this $10,000,000 in other directions. Comparisons would be useless in face of the fact that we are all aware that this money is not being given in the public interest, but for the purpose of settling an old score with my hon. friend on the other side who is so prominent in this matter. My purpose in rising was to place myself on record against this measure, and to enter my protest against this measure, which I regard as the most unjustifiable proposal that was ever made in the Canadian Parliament.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOT-BINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
(Translation.) (Mr. Chairman, before the Bill carries I wish to give my opinion on the matter now being discussed and reply to my hon. friend from Guys'borough (Mr. Sinclair), who has registered a protest against the measure now before this House.
I want to place on record that I am in favour of the Government proposal regarding the Quebec and Saguenay railway.

I understand that the subsidizing of that Toad dates back to a period previous to the advent of this Government. Many years ago subsidies were voted, but conditions became such that the work had to be delayed for a time. It must be said that the enterprise was launched in proper time, but there came a stringency which resulted in the work being suspended.
I am free to state that the hon. member from Charlevoix (Sir Rodolphe Forget), who is a man of note in the province of Quebec, a French Canadian who has reached a foremost place in the world of finance, has undoubtedly helped in a great measure the development of the province of Quebec by different schemes, some of which he has himself launched, and others which he has pro,moted with all the energy for which he is noted. But if this proposal anent the Quebec and Saguenay railway is before this House it cannot be said to be in recognition of political services rendered, because the- question had been agitated long before this Government came into power: As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Charlevoix had undertaken, in common with people from the city of Quebec, to put through this, railway scheme in order to help the people of Charlevoix, who are cut off during winter from the rest of the world on account of their particular situation. Furthermore, the idea was to show that it was possible to secure a winter port on the coast of the province of Quebec as elsewhere in Canada. That is the point I especially want to make. Is the scheme nothing but a dream, or is it feasible? This Government, by their policy incorporated in the Bill now before the House, have solved the question.
That policy was entered into by the late Government, and the present Administration now seeks the means to carry it out. Should this great undertaking materialize it will open up for the province of Quebec immense commercial possibilities.
Some hon. gentlemen, during this debate, have raised doubts as to the possibility of winter navigation on the St. Lawrence. I Will not deny any of my fellow-members the right of giving their opinions on that point, but I have the honour to represent a constituency part of which, the Saguenay district, is deeply interested in that road, because that district extends over the whole north shore from Tadoussac to Belle-Isle.
I know that seven years ago the Department of Marine had a special survey made of the ice situation on the St. Lawrence be-

tween Belle-Isle and Murray Bay, on the north shore, and Cape Race and river Ouelle, on the south shore, in order to determine the possibility of winter navigation on the St. Lawrence. The survey was continued the next winter, and demonstrated clearly-the report is on file at the Department of Marine-that for 98 per cent of the season the north channel is open, because during winter the prevailing wind blows from the north, and, of course, drives- the ice against the south shore. I have not to-night the official reports here, but anyone can see them at the Department of Marine.
For a century previous to the last twenty-five or thirty years the fishermen of the north shore, in small wooden schooners, more or less seaworthy, used to make their way every winter through the ice floes of the St. Lawrence in search of the sea-wolf; they came back with a fair catch and without ever an accident. At that time the price of oil made the venture a paying one. But twenty-five or thirty years ago, I think I said, oil so dropped in price that the fishermen, who could no more make a living out of it, quit that pursuit, which was reputed dangerous. In the last few years the price of oil rose up considerably, and the fishermen put to sea again after the sea-wolf.
This morning I had a letter from one of the leading men of Sept-Iles, stating that the fishermen had just returned to the village, after a three-months' cruise through the St. Lawrence floes, with a catch of 35,000 sea wolves, without having encountered the least danger; the trip means a haul worth about $200,000.
When the poor fishermen-I mean no disparagement-with their meagre means, can encounter 'in the gulf the dangers of the ice floes the best part of the winter to earn their living and their families' without any loss of life or vessel, is- there not sufficient reason for this Government to introduce a Bill with the aim of solving the important problem of winter navigation on the St. Lawrence? True it is these are war times, but the war will not be everlasting, at least so' we hope, and, when the end comes we have reason to hope that Canadian trade and industry will spring into renewed life; should not, therefore, the Government get ready to meet the new conditions that will arise?
For my part, that is the main motive underlying the Government's policy to-day. They are not paying any debt of gratitude
to the hon. member for Charlevoix; his worth is well known, and requires no tribute from me. We are face to face with a problem which concerns the future of the province of Quebec, which is of the utmost importance, and which will be solved by the Government measure now before the House. ' Therefore I will vote for the measure.
Doubts have been raised as to the possibility of a winter sea port on the St. Law' rence. Let us see. At St. Catherine's bay, the proposed terminus of the Quebec and Saguenay railway, the Government has subsidized for the last twelve years a small wooden steamer, which plies regularly twice a day between Tadoussac and St. Catherine's bay, without the service ever suffering any accidents or delays. This same boat has, moreover, taken successful trips, four to eight per month, from Tadoussac to Fraserville, on the south shore, a distance of thirty miles. At that point, the crossing being further east, is considered more difficult than the crossing between Murray bay and river Ouelle.
Every one knows that the straits of Belle Isle are open all winter. The surveying party I have spoken of have reported that the northwest channel, in the Belle Isle straits, are always open to navigation. Now, if account is taken of the additional protection afforded by the vessels, and different points along the coast being provided with the wireless, thus- providing telegraphic communications with the Government line on the north shore, it will be understood that at any time the captains of vessels can always be warned of the presence of ice floes and be given information as to the state of the channel; in that way all possible safety is insured. '
As a result of the enactment of this Bill the city of Quebec will become, through the contemplated railway, a winter terminus, which, compared with other Canadian winter ports, will shorten the distance to Europe by several hundred miles, to the general benefit of the country, and especially to the benefit of the city of Quebec, the capital of my province, and a subject of pride to all French Canadians.
Those considerations demonstrate the unfairness of the suggestions made here, and spread throughout the country by party OTgans that the only object of the Government is to be kind to its political friends and reward the hon. member for Charlevoix for services rendered. The Administration's sole purpose is to do justice by Quebec and

to build new roads, shorter and easier roads, for the large trade that Canada may expect after the war, I must congratulate the Government on the courage it has shown, at the present juncture, in having had the courage to put through this undertaking.
If the Quebec and Saguenay railway weTe a mere convenience for the people of Quebec and Charlevoix, the scheme might be open to objection, but the terminus at St. Catherine's gives it national importance for Canadian trade. The Government's policy looks to the whole country and is nothing if not national. All those reasons should secure its acceptance without further discussion.	*
I noticed that the right hon. leader of the Opposition has departed from the position taken by some of his followers, and appears to favour the project. I congratulate him on his stand.

speechtext:
I am afraid I am in
the same box as the acting Minister oi Railways, in not being able to follow very closely the hon. member for Chicoutimi and Saguenay; but I take it for granted that he was not criticising the railway policy of the late Government.
In those days we remembered his association with that party and his love and fidelity to the Laurier Government. If anybody was to receive consideration with regard to this railway, as has been hinted by my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), when considerations were being passed around, I would not be surprised if the hon. member for Chicoutimi and Saguenay (Mr. Girard) heard something about it. I understand that in the latter days of the last election he saw a great

light, and that all of a sudden the things that were beautiful and strong and good became everything that was dark and dreary and forbidding. Posters and manifestos setting forth his real and true heart up to election day were immediately scored off, and a new proposition was submitted to the people of the county. If the hon. gentleman who is supposed to be leader, and whom my hon. friend from Guysborough referred as the leader, of the Nationalist party, has made any proposition to the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, I would ask him to be cautious, to carry out this part of the deal, if deal it ba. on the instalment plan, and to be pretty careful about his sinking fund, because this hon. gentleman will not stay bought.
With that preliminary information, I simply wish to put myself on record, like my hon. friend from Guysborough, in regard to this railway. The right hon. the Prime Minister knows better than any other hon. gentleman sitting on that side of the House our attitude towards railway building in eastern Canada, particularly in .Nova Scotia. During the years 1908-9-10-11 the then leader of the Opposition, now the Prime Minister, and the members from eastern Nova Scotia, were pulling on the same oar for the purpose of getting railway extensions in that part of Nova Scotia. We succeeded in 1911 in having an amount of money granted by this Parliament for the purpose of certain railway extensions in that province. Everybody from Nova Scotia was satisfied, and things went along first rate. The moneys were voted for Victoria, the county which I have the honour to represent, the county of Halifax, represented by the then leader of the Opposition, and the counties of Pictou and Guysborough, represented by the hon. gentlemen who represent them to-day. But what a change has taken place in the policy of the right hon. gentleman in reg,ard to the building of railways! I have on several occasions taunted the Prime Minister with having built his own railway and having left us out. I think he should have built the railways in Guysborough, Pictou and Victoria, because we were all pulling together, and I suppose the fact that he was pulling with us helped to get the Government of that day, the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, to commit themselves to the policy of building these roads. Without repeating that charge too often, I submit that when one of the roads went on, the road in Halifax county from Dean Settlement to Dartmouth, they

all should have been placed in the same category and dealt with in the same way. However, matters, have gone otherwise. In 1912, 1913 and so on, we were told that it was only a matter of a short time when the same policy would be carried out in the other counties. In the county of -Victoria, the gentleman who ran against me in 1911, the candidate of my right hon. friend, and those who were supporting him, said: Do not vote for Mackenzie, because it would procure this railway; but defeat Mackenzie and defeat the Government and the road will be built all the same. The Conservatives in Victoria believed that, stood to their guns and voted for that gentleman. But they have discovered since that the promises made to them were not carried out by the Government and party which they supported. I, and other gentlemen, have been told during the last two years that proposals of this kind could not be carried forward because the finances of the country could not stand it on account of war conditions. That is a fair proposition, that is something that -we can tell our people and the people can understand. The Government have found it necessary to put extraordinary taxation on the poor people of this country, taxes that they can ill afford to pay. We might very well understand that new enterprises would be allowed to stand until we were better off than we are to-day. But this is a new proposition. There was never a word of this railway during the later years of the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I never heard the Prime Minister, when he vas leader of the Opposition, or any of his friends- from Quebec, or any other part of Canada, put this forward or mention this road as a scheme that we might look forward to as a part of the railway system of Canada. There was never one word about it.
Now, it is most extraordinary that railways which were expecting to receive consideration years ago, and for which moneys were voted unanimously by both sides of this House, are passed over, forgotten and neglected, and a new proposition altogether is brought forward which is going to involve an expenditure of some $10,000,000. When an expenditure of this kind is proposed, it gives colour to the statements made by my hon. friend from Guysborough. It looks as if some sinster motive, some reason more urgent than the building of an ordinary piece of road, were behind it, when the Prime Minister and his Government break away from a line of policy that
they have laid out for themselves in the last two or three years and come in asking for an expenditure of this kind. I can only tell the people of Victoria that the Government of the day and the Prime Minister broke faith With them, that they did not carry out their promise to them, and that other people were stronger in the affections and regard of the Prime Minister than they are, for some reason unexplainable to me except that which was set forth by my hon. friend from Guysborough. Whether it is true or not, I suppose we shall not be able to find out1; but there is no other satisfactory reason. This reason having been given, I am content to leave it there until some more satisfactory one is afforded. We have for thg past few years been leaving public works in different parts of Nova Scotia idle and dormant, and no progress has been made.
We were not asking for them to be built, because we were told there was no money. I am sure I am within the mark when I say that there are dozens of places in the county I have the honour to represent where an expenditure of public money is more needed, and would be more in the general interests of Canada than the expenditures which the Government are making to-day, not only in connection with railways, but other public wmrks. But we have been silent because we thought the Government did not have the money and were in earnest when they said that nothing could be done, as all our energies and all our finances had to be concentrated on the main purpose, the winning of the war. It looks now as if the poor people were to be taxed not only for the war, but for other purposes that were never mentioned when the war taxes were imposed, and when explanations were given in that connection not only by the Prime Minister, but by the Minister of Finance.
My purpose in rising was to protest against the Government going on with a work of this character when other under takings of a like character which had the inside track, so to speak, and which were spoken of long before there was ever a word said iabout this road, were more urgently needed. I submit that when any thing of this character is undertaken by the Government the question of going on with all these other branches should be considered at the same time. They should all be dealt with under the same policy, sc that all sections of eastern Canada where' railway extensions of this kind are neces-



sary should receive the same consideration and at the same time. I am not saying that these people in Quebec should not have this railway; I am not saying anything about that; I assume that they should have it. But' not a whit more do they require railway facilities, not as much indeed, ae the people in the county of Victoria who live, not thirty or forty, but some places over a hundred and twenty miles away from a railway, and in which county are some of the oldeet settlements in America. After I have been pressing hard to get these people a road, and when I had hopes at one time that all the provisions were made and that the road was at hand, you will pardon me, Mr. Chairman, if I feel disappointed now that I see we have been passed over, and other places-not a bit more deserving receiving the consideration which is given by this Bill and by the vote which it involves.
Mr. LEMIiETJX:	The right hon. the
Prime Minister was not in his seat this afternoon when I was speaking on this Bill. Of course, I understand that he is very busy and cannot be here every moment; 'but now that he is here I wish to make an appeal to him, for I look on him as a friend of France. I stated very briefly this afternoon that I opposed the Government in acquiring the line from Lyster to St. Jean des Chaillons and the line from Quebec to St. Joachim, but upheld the aid to the line from St. Joachim to Nairn Falls, as I thought it would he better to do something towards the completion of that road. However, the Government has decided to acquire these lines, and the Acting Minister of Railways ha6 stated that the bondholders will he paid at par for their holdings. I asked whether the bondholders in France, who had sold their bonds at below par, would be allowed the difference between the price they sold at and what they had originally paid, and the answer was in the negative. The reason why I insist upon the right hon. gentleman taking a favourable view of this question is this: as I stated this afternoon, aild as was confirmed by the hon. member for Charlevoix, nearly all the money for the construction of that section of the line from St. Joachim, in the county of Montmorency, to Nairn Falls, was obtained in the French financial market. The hon. member for Charlevoix stated this afternoon that $1,000,000 odd had been subscribed in Canada, and $4,600,000 in the ' 
French market. To be accurate, I must istate that the bonds were sold at 82. Later on, when the French bondholders, got discouraged at the failure of the company, they were induced to sell their bonds at a low figure; this was not denied. These bonds were bought up by a Canadian group of financiers, and, if I understand the situation correctly, this group will be paid the face value Of the bonds which they secured at so low a figure. The reason why the Canadian Government should view with favour the suggestion I make is this and I direct the attention of the right hon. gentleman particularly to this: first of all, we are the allies of France, and we must play fair in our financial dealings with them; secondly, this money was secured after some very alluring prospectuses had.'been issued on the French market-; nobody will deny that. Among the names that appeared on one prospectus was that of an ex-member of this Government, the late Postmaster General, the Hon. Mr. Pelletier. It is true that after a while bis name disappeared from the prospectus because he found it inconsistent with his position as a minister of the Grown to figure in any financial venture in a foreign market. Among the inducements which were held out to French investors, they were told, for instance-and it was quite an inducement-that this line of railway would run not merely to Nairn Falls, or even to St. Catherine's hay, hut as far as Cape St. Charles, on the Labrador coast.
This was a great inducement; for they were told that the ocean trip between Europe and Canada would be greatly shortened; that in three days at most the steamers would cross the ocean and would reach the terminus of this railway. All this, stated in the prospectus, no doubt did much to influence French investors to put their money into this enterprise. Another inducement which certainly had its effect in getting money from the-French investor is to be found in the statement of the assets and the revenue of the company, which was published broadcast. It was stated that a subsidy of $400,000 would be paid by the Dominion Government, and that the land subsidy from the provincial Government was valued at $840,000. As to the revenues of the road, it was stated that 160,000-passengers would be carried at $1 per passenger, giving an annual revenue of $160,000. It was stated also that the road would command freight traffic to the amount of
420,000	tons, yielding a revenue of $630,000. The expenditure was represented to be only

$528,000, leaving a net profit for the investors of $264,000. Now, I quite understand that this was only a calculation made by the Canadian promotors. JBut here is wheie the Government, it seems to me, is morally responsible for the inducements offered to the French investor.

They were told that this little bit of a road from St. Joachim to Nairn Falls was practically another transcontinental railway; that it would run as far as Cape Charles on the Labrador coast. It was on the assumption that this road would be built that they invested their money. I must say that it is not the first time that that has happened. We have heard the history of the Chignecto railway; I do not know whether the member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) has heard of that scheme. I suppose that every year the right hon. gentleman sees a ghost in the person of a certain gentleman who represents the bondholders of the Chig-aecto Ship railway, who has been waiting very patiently for the last thirty or thirty-five years. speechtext:
It is hardly
necessary to appeal to any one in Canada on the score of the relations between our Empire and France at the present time. We all know that these relations are of the warmest character, and we are giving very good evidence of that in this country through the splendid expeditionary force which is fighting for the liberties of France as well as for those of the Empire in the battle-line at the front at the present time. When my hon. friend suggests that we should enter into some inquiry with a view of making good to all persons who have become interested in the bonds of this railway the amount that they may have originally invested, he asks the Government. to embark upon a proposal that would have very far-reaching consequences. On various occasions when I have visited Great Britain during the past ten or twelve years I found people over there who had invested in some enterprise in Canada which had not proved remunerative. Many of these persons would have been, glad to get even 10 cents on the dollar in respect of some of the enterprises into which they had put their money. I have no doubt that my hon. friend himself can look back and see in the course of his career some investments made by him in respect of iwhiefr he would be very glad to get 10 or 25 cents on the dollar to-day. If a paternal Government would come to his .assistance and make that good, I have no doubt that he would be very much gratified; but he could hardly expect it. This road runs [through an old, long-settled 'Community which is shut out from all communication with the world for five or six months of the year. The late Administration gave this enterprise its sanction and its imprimatur by granting it a subsidy. The .Legislature of Quebec did the same thing

under the condition that the enterprise .should be somewhat greater than that which we have now under consideration, and should extend to a point farther down the coast. A great deal of money was invested in the construction of the road, and for the last three or four years all the money so invested has lain absolutely idle. .More than that, the work which it represents has been deteriorating from year to year. So that the prospect of having the enterprise, as originally proposed, completed for the benefit of those people, .has seemed to be getting farther and farther .away. The late Administration or this Administration would no doubt have been very glad if those who had invested their money in the enterprise in the first instance, when they realized that there was not enough money to finish it, had undertaken the burden of completing it, taking .the chance of saving their money to the fullest extent by making it a success. But there was no disposition of that kind. *There has been no attempt on the part of bondholders, so far as I am aware, to raise money for the purpose of completing the road, and it has been in the condition which I have described from year to year. Under the circumstance, it did not seem desirable in the interests either of the district or of the whole country that an enterprise of this kind, designed to serve a very considerable community in a district which had been settled so long, should be almost nine-tenths completed and remain in that condition for a number of years to come. ,We were not prepared to embark upon the proposal which my hon. friend suggests, which would have involved a great deal more money, perhaps twice as much as we are proposing to expend. My hon. friend observes the reception which our more .modest proposal has had from some of his friends on that side of the House We were not prepared to embark upon that plan; but we were prepared to propose to the House that what might be called the reasonable value of the road should be paid, and that the road should be completed and made to serve the purpose for which it was originally designed .by the late Admin,-istration when it subsidized the road and by the Government of the province of Quebec when it extended aid. The proposal which we make to the House is in effect that the reasonable value of the road, a certain sum of money not exceeding the amount named in the Bill, should be paid for the road, and that in determining that sum
the cost of the road and subsequent depreciation should be taken into consideration.
I regret that we could not go to the extent that the hon. member for Rouville suggests. The proposal which the Government has submitted to the House is designed, on the one hand, to do justice, so far as justice can be done, to those who are the holders of the securities, by paying the reasonable value of the road, and, on the other hand, to carry out the proposal as it was first sanctioned by Parliament, involving the completion of this line in order that it may serve the purpose for which it was originally intended. That, in a word, is the proposal of the Government, and it is. one, .which, it -seems to me, ought to command the approval of hon. members. I do not wish the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) and the hon. member for North	Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr.	McKenzie),	to imagine
that the interests of the communities to which they have referred have been overlooked or will be forgotten. This enterprise stands in this position. It had been sanctioned by the late Administration; it had been subsidized, it had been endowed with a subsidy Dy the Provincial Government, and a very large sum of money had been expended upon it. Yet the road was lying as an uncompleted affair, of absolutely no use to any person in the world in the condition in which it has been during the past three years. More than that, it was deteriorating all the time by the action of the elements, making it worth less and less each year. For these reasons the Government, while it would have greatly preferred that the persons interested in the road * should come forward and undertake the additional burden necessary to complete it and make it a success, nevertheless, seeing fhat that apparently could not be done thought Parliament should interpose in the ,way now proposed by this Bill and should .complete a road which has been lying almost completed for three or four years.

speechtext:
I forgot to point out that I think the sending of this to the Exchequer Court is not a very good way to arrive at the price. We all know that judges are honourable men and desirous of doing the very best they can; but, while a judge may be a good lawyer, he is not a rail. road man. As a rule, he knows nothing about the construction of railways, nothing about engineering, and, taking it all in all, it is a fair proposition to say that judges are not railway men. I cannot understand why a railroad, particularly one of this kind that is in a half-finished condition, and one that has been allowed to deteriorate for the last few years, with the embank-

ments wearing away, should be submitted to a judge for valuation. Where the railroad was raised to grade level some years ago, no doubt these grades have washed away; and I am sure I am right when I say that no part of that road is up to grade now. I know something about the grading of a railway, and I am sure that a railroad, particularly on an embankment, that was graded four years ago and since then has been subject to the upheavals of frost and the action of weather, etc., is nothing like up to grade. I venture to say it is in very poor condition. We are going to ask a judge to take into consideration all these things which appertain particularly to the judgment of a railway man. I would suggest that the Railway Department, with any assistance they might wish to obtain, would be far more capable than a judge sitting alone to determine the proper value of this road. I submit further that human nature is human nature. Who are the two sides to this controversy about this road's value? Who are fighting it out? We have the Prime Minister and his colleagues fighting their friends. They have clearly come to the assistance of their friends in this case. They are willing to give them money to help them out.
Atc they going to fight them very vigorously when they get before the man who is to name the amount? I have seen these trials before. I have seen judges with the very best intentions trying to arrive at the true value of lands taken for right of way when politicians were concerned in the value of the lands, and when it was impossible for the judge to get evidence because nobody would give it; nobody was anxious to cut down the value of the land. Those representing the Government were anxious 'that the politicians who owned that land should get big value for it, and no witnesses were put- on the stand at all. This House should have the strongest assurance that this action, for -action it is, will be properly defined and placed before the judge, and that the issues, in one form or another, will be fought out. We should have the assurance that this matter is to be fought out the same as if the party w'h-o is going to get the money were not a -friend and supporter of the Government.

speechtext:
So far as ascertaining the value- is concerned, the evidence of experts must-, of course, be given. If the Government undertook to fix the value themselves, my hon. friend realizes, and has indeed said, that their estimate would

depend on the valuation of persons who are familiar with such matters. Members of a government could not personally undertake to value such a road. In arriving at the value the Judge of the Exchequer Court will have to depend, I suppose, on testimony of the same kind. The hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria says he would prefer to have the Minister of Railways and Canals fix the value. We thought it would be fairer and more reasonable, un-,der all the circumstances, that a Judge of the Exchequer Court should fix it. That is very frequently done by a government, even in cases where the value is less difficult of determination than in the present case. For example, one of the latest acts of the late Administration was to pass an Order in Council by which certain land in the suburbs of Calgary, belonging to the Northwest Mounted Police, should be transferred to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. The Government did not undertake to fix the value themselves; they directed that it should be referred to the Exchequer Court of Canada for valuation. Unfortunately, they had overlooked the fact that the1 Exchequer Court of Canada had no jurisdiction to do anything of the kind, and so we had to take the matter up at a somewhat later date. The only way in which the matter could be worked out was to appoint one of the Exchequer Court judges as arbitrator for the purpose of estimating the value, and that course was taken. We agreed with our predecessors that it was better that the value should be fixed by a judge of the Exchequer Court as valuator than that the Government should attempt to determine it themselves. There was the question of prospective value and considerations of that character, which it would have been unfortunate, probably, for the Government to determine; and so in this case. I think there are considerations connected with the value of the road and the reasonable price to be paid for it which, under the circumstances, might better be determined by a judicial inquiry than by the Government themselves.

maintopic: QUEBEC AND SAGUENAY AND LOT-BINIERE AND MEGANTIC RAILWAYS.
speechtext:
I agree with my hon.
friend that the tribunal of the Exchequer Court would be a very good one to determine the value if that question were left to the judge of the Exchequer Court. But it is not. If my right hon. friend will look at the amendment he will see that the judge of the Exchequer Court has not a word to say about the value. He is simply to take
the cost,>
and, so long as the cost does not exceed $6,849,000, he is bound to allow it under the statute. That obligation is imposed on the judge; there is not the slightest discretion left to him to determine the value. To my mind, it is the most extraordinary proceeding which I have ever seen taken. Parliament purports tq leave to the Exchequer Court the fixing of the value, and then tells the judge of the Exchequer Court how he is to fix the value-that he is to take the cost, whether it is twice or three times the value of the property, and be governed by that cost provided it does not exceed a certain amount. Section 2, as amended, would read as follows:
The consideration to be paid for each of the said railways and for any equipment, appurtenances and properties that may he acquired as aforesaid shall be the value thereof as determined by the Exchequer Court of Canada.
That would have been all right if the section had been left there. That would have met the view which my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has presented to the committee, as .affording a good reason why the judge of the ' Exchequer Court should be appointed to deal with the matter. But the amendment proposed bjr the Acting Minister of Railways ties the hands of the judge of the Exchequer Court in this manner:
The said value to be the actual cost of said railways, less subsidies and less depreciation, but not to exceed $4,349,000 exclusive of outstanding bonded indebtedness, which is to be assumed by the Government, but not to exceed in all $2,500,000.
My right hon. friend will see that if the total cost, less depreciation and less subsidies, does not exceed $6,849,000, the judge of the Exchequer Court must, allow this company that amount of money even although, in his own opinion, the value of the road is not one-third of that amount. That is the objection which I see to this amendment. The very first thing to do-no doubt it was the first thing which the Minister of Railways thought of doing when the proposition was made by this company to sell these railroads to the Government- was to refer the matter to the General Manager of Government Railways; and it is a very singular fact that there is no recommendation of the general manager in respect to the taking over of these three roads. But the matter was referred by him, evidently at once, to his chief engineer, and the chief engineer, Mr. Beckwith, made an examination of these three lines of rail-

way. The structural value of what is called the Quebec and Montmorency line, that is the line which is in operation, is put at $1,115,200, and that includes the terminals, equipment, the whale completed railway. That is the value which is fixed by the Government's own engineer. My hon. friend will find it on page 6 of the report made by Mr. Beckwith to Mr. Brown, the Chief Engineer of Government Railways at Moncton. But I understand that that line is bonded for $2,500,000, and, presumably, that is the cost which the company will be able to show to the judge of the Exchequer Court.
Then, if we take the Quebec and Saguenay part, the engineer in his report, which was submitted to the Government by Mr. Brown, the Chief Engineer of Government Railways, puts the total value of that property at $2,813,500.
There we get the valuation of these two principal roads, made by the engineering department of the Government railways at a little over $3,928,000. Then, if you take the small road on the south side of the St. Lawrence, the statement of the engineer is that the fair cost would be $466,000, of which subsidies were received to the extent of $240,000, leaving $220,000 as the money which was put into the road. If you take the total cost of $466,000, you have about $4,300,000 as being the value of these three lines of railway, or as being the amount of money which it would cost to construct them when this report was made in 1915. Yet this amendment requires the judge of the Exchequer Court to allow these companies, not what the engineering department says they are -worth, but if it is shown that they have cost that much, the judge is bound to allow them $6,949,000, or $2,600,000 more than the engineering department of the Government railways declares these roads are worth. This is not proper legislation. Surely the judge of the Exchequer Court ought to be allowed to call witnesses before him and the Government ought to be able to submit evidence. The judge of the Exchequer Court ought to be permitted to allow the companies what these three roads are fairly worth. So far from that being the case, his hands are tied, and if these companies show the judge that the cost may have been $6,949,000, the judge is bound to allow that enormous sum when the roads ought to have cost only what the engineer states. In other words, the judge is not limited to the fair or necessary value or cost, but is bound to allow them $6,949,000 even al-

though that amount is $2,600,000 more than the Government's own engineer says is the value of these three railways.
On the preamble:

.Minister of Railways told us a moment ago ,that it was not the Government's intention to extend this railway farther than Murray jBay. Is it the intention to at once proceed with the completion of the road?

There is no
appropriation for it in the Estimates.
